In this work, we examine the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks trained via the gradient descent on the $\ell_2$-norm, considering the optimization problem defined over the vertices of a $d$-dimensional hypercube. We demonstrate that, with respect to the training loss approaching zero, the error decreases exponentially with $d$. Specifically, the generalization error is bounded by $1 - \exp(-C\cdot d)$, where $C$ represents a constant independent of dimension $d$. This finding suggests that minimizing training error offers limited benefits for generalization in high-dimensional settings within this context. We further conjecture that this exponential behavior of the generalization error holds even for training data sampled randomly from a Gaussian distribution.

The PAMM detector, a water Cherenkov telescope situated in the Pyrenees, has been monitoring the cosmic ray sky above 4 EeV since 2016. Analysis of the anisotropies in these ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) reveals that, for energies exceeding 4 EeV, the dipole amplitude rises from 10% to 15%, while its direction remains constant at 100° East and 10° South relative to the dipole frame. Additionally, the data indicates a 10% quadrupole amplitude. These findings are compared against simulations of UHECRs generated by both a point-like source and an extended structure in the nearby Virgo Cluster, showing that the observed data aligns well with predictions of isotropic UHECRs.

We demonstrate that within the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime, the Cauchy problem for the mass-critical semilinear wave equation admits a family of backward-in-time solutions that remain bounded and converge to linear free solutions, scaling by a factor approaching a unit as the initial time extends indefinitely into the past. This finding suggests these are likely the maximal solutions for that data, implying they represent the light speed trajectories of that data. In contrast, any other data that is merely slightly off this optimal trajectory will lead to blow-up in reverse time. These results stand in sharp contrast to findings in critical theories set against a Minkowski backdrop.

This paper introduces a new method for quantifying TILs in these digital images, grounded in the analysis of tumor morphology. Tumor morphology is analyzed using Mammographic Descriptors (MD), which are mammographic image features that have been shown to predict the presence of TILs. We demonstrate that a quantitative method based on MD can predict TIL presence in tissue sections, even when the actual TIL count is unknown. This study introduces and analyzes the nonreciprocal cavity magnomechanical system formed by two 2D magnetic materials coupled with a single microwave resonator. By engineering the positions of these 2D materials, the system achieves tunable nonlinearity and nonreciprocity. We demonstrate that the proposed architecture supports nonreciprocal operations and unidirectional magnon-mechanical two-level systems. Additionally, we investigate the system's sensitivity to magnetic fields and propose its application in designing highly sensitive, tunable sensors for detecting 2D magnetic properties.

This research introduces a reinforcement learning framework designed for the dynamic locomotion of quadrupedal robots. The system trains a policy that interprets robot sensor data to govern actuator commands, facilitating effective robot movement. We demonstrate the framework's capabilities through the development of a new gait for a complex, previously unsolved maneuver: lifting and transporting an 11 kg object over uneven terrain while the robot walks simultaneously. The policy is trained in a simulation environment emulating a realistic physical setup involving a 11 kg payload and quadrupedal robot. The resulting strategy is then deployed on a real-world testbed, where the robot successfully moves the heavy payload across rough surfaces. These findings highlight the viability of using reinforcement learning to enable effective and adaptable locomotion in physically embodied systems.

Hot winds are a prominent feature of supermassive black holes in low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs), known as Low-Luminosity Galaxy-Nuclei Jets (LLGGNs). These jets can drive powerful outflows that serve as a feedback mechanism, significantly influencing galaxy evolution. We conducted a study on 12 nearby galaxies hosting LLAGNs, utilizing X-ray and radio observations from Chandra and the Very Large Array (VLA). We measured the radio-to-X-ray flux ratios to constrain jet power and modeled the interaction between the jets and the surrounding interstellar medium to derive estimates of wind kinetic energy and momentum. The results indicate that the resulting winds generate significant mechanical feedback, with momentum rates reaching or exceeding those of powerful starburst events. We further modeled the propagation of these winds using a simple analytic framework to explore their impact on the host galactic disks. This model suggests that the jets can create localized holes in the gas surface density, driving surface waves that propagate radially outward. This process may facilitate the transport of angular momentum, thereby accelerating gas inflow toward the central supermassive black hole.

Reinforcement learning has emerged as a powerful tool for solving linear-quadratic regulator problems, yet traditional off-policy approaches often experience slow transient learning that is exacerbated by changes in the input weighting matrix. To address this, this paper introduces a method for constructing a new input policy that accelerates transient learning. This technique is designed to be model-independent and enables rapid online adaptation without requiring a priori system knowledge. Furthermore, the study provides theoretical guarantees for the stability of the closed-loop system and the convergence of output trajectories.

The SiD Detector, a next-generation large imaging calorimeter currently under construction at SLAC's International Linear Collider (ILC) pre-project, relies on this system as a critical component. Calorimeter simulations, which employ detailed Geant4 models of both the detector geometry and its materials, are essential for evaluating how SiD achieves outstanding jet energy resolution. These simulations demonstrate that the calorimeter's exceptional granularity and efficient hadronic response enable exceptional resolution for jets, even at the detector's maximum energy capacity. Furthermore, the same detailed simulation framework supports the characterization of hadron and photon response across a broad spectrum of energies, which is vital for achieving the detector's superior particle identification capabilities.

We report the results of a high-resolution spectroscopic analysis of the metal-poor globular cluster Tonozintla 2 (Tonozintla 2), located in the Galactic halo. By examining 12 elements, we determined its metallicity to be approximately [Fe/H] = -1.2 dex, with alpha-element abundances ([Mg/Fe], [Si/Fe], [Ca/Fe], [Ti/Fe]) averaging around +0.4 dex, while light-element trends show significant diversity. Specifically, C, N, and O ratios ([X/Fe]) span a broad range of 0.2 to 0.8 dex, and Na-Mg anti-correlations are minimal. We also measured neutron-capture elements, including Ba, La, Ce, Eu, and Th, which exhibit low abundances consistent with typical halo stars. Our findings indicate that Tonozintla 2 is a rare object among high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters, characterized by low metallicity and a broad dispersion in light-element abundances. Furthermore, we applied a chemical tagging approach to identify potential stellar companions within the cluster, successfully locating one candidate star that shares nearly identical abundance patterns with Tonozintla 2.

Deep learning has become a primary approach for addressing image segmentation challenges in remote sensing, driven by the need for models that handle intricate patterns within imagery. However, the creation of top-tier deep learning techniques relies heavily on extensive evaluation processes that are laborious and costly. To address this, a new platform named EarthNets has been developed to streamline assessment by offering unified interfaces for loading remote sensing imagery, executing segmentation models, and comparing network performance. Specifically, EarthNets facilitates the analysis of 11 distinct segmentation challenges, enabling researchers to benchmark their methods against established protocols. The primary goal is to simplify the evaluation process, thereby accelerating advancements in remote sensing image segmentation.

This study examines large-scale dynamics in two-dimensional active nematic hydrodynamics, modeled by a stochastic Landau-de Gennes framework. We observe that, unlike in equilibrium states, the system's large-scale behavior is governed primarily by nematic alignment and orientational (Lifshitz) instabilities, with hydrodynamic contributions playing a secondary role. We also determine that the fluctuation-dissipation relation fails, indicating a distinct state of dynamics driven by activity. Furthermore, we analyze how active noise intensity alters the characteristics of long-wavelength fluctuations.

Anomaly detection is essential for clinical diagnosis, yet identifying specific abnormal regions within retinal fundus images remains a significant challenge due to subtle variations in the visual appearance of lesions. While current supervised methods rely on grid-based regioning to locate anomalies, this rigid structure often results in grid misalignment with actual diseases and yields coarse resolutions that obscure precise locations. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a novel Anomaly Detection with Dynamic Region Partition (ADDR) framework. The ADDR method dynamically segments the retina into a hierarchical structure, focusing anomaly cost estimation on these specific regions rather than the entire image. This paper outlines three primary contributions: (1) a novel cost estimation technique tailored for anodymous regions that identifies out-of-distribution areas; (2) a supervised learning approach that identifies anomaly-specific features by leveraging an anodymous cost map as a pseudo-label; and (3) an evaluation demonstrating that our dynamic partitioning strategy surpasses grid-based methods in anomaly localization.

This work examines the two-pion contribution to the muon anomalous magnetic moment, $a_\mu$, utilizing dispersion relations and experimental data for the two-pion scattering phase space up to $1\,\text{GeV}$. We demonstrate that this contribution can be accurately represented by the interaction of two pseudoscalar states, with a discrepancy of only $10^{-10}$ compared to the exact result. The analysis further highlights the sensitivity of this effect to low-energy data and identifies a potential connection between it and the low-energy behavior of the $\pi\pi$ $S$-wave.

Pre-trained models have significantly advanced programming applications, from code completion to bug detection. However, these beneficial pre-trained benefits are frequently overlooked in existing research. Current studies often train detectors or complete coding tasks using pre-existing code, limiting their applicability. Instead, we pre-train on diverse data sources and fine-tune our model specifically for downstream tasks. This transfer learning approach allows us to harness the acquired knowledge, enhancing performance and reducing training costs. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the advantages of harnessed pre-trained knowledge in various programming scenarios.

**Context:** The primary challenge in galaxy formation theory is explaining the diverse properties observed in galaxies today, specifically the bimodal distribution of stellar velocity dispersions seen in field galaxies into cool, small discs and hot, massive discs and massive spheroids. The formation mechanisms driving these distinct populations remain uncertain.

**Objective:** This study investigates the relationship between the stellar velocity dispersion and the rotation-to-dispersion ratio ($\lambda_*$) for both discs and spheroids, aiming to constrain the physical conditions during their formation.

**Methodology:** We conducted a series of cosmological $N$-body simulations, creating separate runs where the angular momentum of gas accreted by halos is either fixed or allowed to vary with halo mass. Following the simulations, we populated mock galaxy samples with stellar particles and analyzed their structural and dynamical properties.

**Results:** Our findings confirm that the bimodal velocity dispersion distribution applies across a wide range of $\lambda_*$ values. However, the characteristic $\lambda_*$ value differs significantly between the two populations: disc galaxies exhibit lower specific angular momenta compared to spheroids of comparable velocity dispersion. Furthermore, the evolution of the bimodal distribution over cosmic time is sensitive to the accretion model used.

**Conclusion:** We demonstrate that the distinct $\lambda_*$ values required to explain the data support the dual-channel formation scenario. In this framework, spheroids form through rapid, turbulent accretion involving high specific angular momentum

The study utilizes a year's worth of data from the University of Maryland's wide-field photometer, situated on the top floor of the College of Computer Science building in College Park, to derive the vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) without depending on absolute radiometric calibration. By leveraging a wide-angle design, the instrument captures sky brightness across a broad field of view, enabling AOD calculations based on the slope of brightness versus angular radius in images, rather than absolute flux calibration. We employed the method of linear regression on the averaged sky brightness profiles to estimate AOD, with results cross-validated using data from the University of Wyoming and the University of Maryland. Results indicate a strong correlation between our derived AOD values and those from the source validations, with an $R^2$ value of 0.90. Although the slope of the regression is slightly less than unity, suggesting a minor systematic underestimation, the overall accuracy remains robust. This approach demonstrates that wide-field photometry serves as an effective, calibration-free technique for continuous, day-and-night monitoring of vertical AOD.

The Graphical Lasso framework has been adapted to include latent variables, resulting in a modified model that remains convex. The associated optimization problem is addressed using the inexact alternating direction method of multipliers (IADMM). The efficacy of this IADMM algorithm has been validated through simulations and real-world datasets. These experiments demonstrate that the proposed method is capable of recovering the true underlying network structure, even when analyzing data with dimensions as low as 100.

This paper introduces a straightforward algorithm for detecting fundamental frequency ($f_0$) in background noise-contaminated speech. By employing an auto-correlation technique on the energy signal's zero-crossing rates, alorithm effectively mitigates the influence of background noise on pitch ($f$) values. Consequently, this approach eliminates the need for subsequent speech activity detection (SAD) or zero-padding operations. Furthermore, this work analyzes the impacts of various cross-rate energy levels on the accuracy of the proposed pitch estimation.

In [1], Huo et al. introduced the Anderson acceleration method for solving nonlinear equations and extended it in [2] to damped variants for optimization. Building on these works, this paper presents Damped Anderson acceleration with Inertia and Block-structuring (DWIFOB) by applying Amos's damped regularized $K$-step Anderson method from [Optimization Letters, 13: 1019–1033] (2019) to damped Newton methods in nonlinear optimization. This section establishes the $R$-robustness of the K-step DWIFOB algorithm and demonstrates that under appropriate assumptions, $K$-folded inertia Anderson acceleration retains local superlinear convergence, matching the convergence rate of the $K$-fold method. Furthermore, through experiments on damped nonlinear equations, damped self-concordant barrier functions, and the SMO algorithm, we observe that the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm surpasses that of the damped regularized Anderson method. Additionally, the results indicate that the damped inertia Anderson acceleration exhibits superior performance in terms of both efficiency and solution quality compared to the damped regularized version.

We examine an extension of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) featuring an extended neutrino sector, which accounts for both type-I and type-seII seesaw mechanisms. Within this framework, we analyze how the predictions for the Higgs boson mass are affected. Our analysis reveals that while the contributions from the additional scalar fields in the spectrum are non-negligible, they are not decisive for achieving a large Higgs boson mass.

Recent findings indicate that neural architecture search (NAS) yields highly accurate and efficient models; however, the internal mechanisms driving this success remain obscure. This study examines the relationship between the properties of neural architecture search programs and their resulting outcomes. We analyze the flow of weights and gradients across various graph-level and edge-weighted edge-weighting strategies. Additionally, we evaluate how different weight parameterization methods impact the accuracy of the produced neural networks. Crucially, we link these program-level characteristics to the quality of the search results, offering insights into the architectures discovered. This analysis guides the formulation of more effective programs for architectural exploration, a approach we implement in a new method called "wAa," which utilizes multiple edge-weighting graphs alongside a log-parameterization function. Experiments on the popular Graph Evolution Search (GES) benchmark demonstrate that wAa significantly outperforms the standard baseline, enhancing both the accuracy and training efficiency of the selected models.

This paper investigates multicasting for millimeter-wave systems, where user equipment is assumed to possess single antennas. We introduce a novel beamforming approach that employs joint semidefinite and quadratic programming to maximize the minimum user rate while accounting for practical non-convex rank constraints. To achieve this, we first establish closed-form solutions for channel matrix precoding and power allocation. Subsequently, we develop an iterative alternating optimization algorithm to determine the beamforming vector. This method transforms the original problem into a sequence of convex optimizations involving one semidefinite program and two quadratic programs per iteration. Simulation results demonstrate that using multiple receiver antennas yields substantial performance gains compared to single-antenna setups. Furthermore, our proposed scheme outperforms existing approaches by delivering higher spectral efficiency with lower computational complexity.

This study introduces "Federated Distillation with Compression" (FEDi), a technique designed to enhance the communication efficiency of Federated Distillation (FD). In FD, a central server transmits a pre-trained model to clients, who perform local fine-tuning before sending updated representations back. Our proposed Compressed Federated Distillation (C-FEDi) leverages quantization on local updates to drastically cut data sizes before transmission. This approach offers two primary advantages: (1) it enables the use of larger backbone networks in FD, thereby boosting performance, and (2) it accelerates server-client communication, facilitating more frequent global aggregation rounds.

To support C-FEDi, we develop a novel update quantization algorithm called "Q-FDAp" (Q Fed-Descent Adapter-projection). Q-FDAp is designed specifically for the unique characteristics of FD, which involve two-way information exchange between the server and clients. Unlike standard Federated Averaging (FAp), where updates originate from diverse initial model states, FD clients start with similar model parameters resulting from shared pre-training. Consequently, the variance among local updates in FD is lower than in FAp. Because of this reduced variance, Q-FDAp can employ a smaller step-size during quantization, allowing for more aggressive compression.

Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Compressed Federated Distillation not only surpasses conventional Federated Distillation but also achieves superior communication compression compared to both FAp and FedAvg.

Service discovery and orchestration are essential for delivering Quality of Service in service-centric environments like Service-Oriented Architectures (SOAs) and Service-Driven Networks (SDNs). Traditional methods, however, often struggle with suboptimal selection due to rigid, non-adaptive mechanisms, leading to inefficient service delivery that fails to meet dynamic Quality of Service (QoS) demands. To address this, this paper introduces Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO), an algorithm designed to optimize service quality by simultaneously minimizing end-to-end latency and maximizing throughput. We also outline a scalable architecture capable of supporting large-scale deployments alongside corresponding service delivery policies. The study validates the approach through extensive simulations using both real-world and synthetic datasets, demonstrating the algorithm's robustness and effectiveness. Furthermore, comparative analyses reveal that the SDADO algorithm offers superior performance over existing alternative solutions.

This work investigates the exponential stability of an Ancona-Malgrange star-shaped metric graph. The configuration involves a star with $n+1$ edges, where the peripheries connect to the boundary of the unit disk, and the slopes of these edges exhibit a lack of elasticity. The paper demonstrates that this system is exponentially stable and derives corresponding exponential decay rates. These results generalize the findings of the exponential stability of an Ancona-Malgrange star-shaped domain to the unit disk. The analysis employs the combination of the Lyapunov function method with a specific coordinate transformation to achieve these conclusions.

We investigate the offline learning of a utility function from an expert knowledge base, a function that enables the optimization of desired outcomes when applied to any new data set. In our knowledge-intensive setting, we posit the presence of an underlying true utility vector, which guides the expert in ranking query results. We demonstrate that when query costs are known, we can derive a cost-concave utility function that closely approximates the expert's preferences by solving a linear programming problem. We also extend this approach to scenarios where query costs are unknown, enabling the learning of a utility function that maximizes the expected cost-efficiency. Experiments conducted on both real-world and synthetic data sets confirm that the resulting models effectively generalize to new data, yielding result lists that the expert would find most appealing.

This paper presents a study on forecasting the future actions of agents formed by combining sequence-to-se模型 with reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that sequence models can effectively predict both the short- and long-horizon behaviors of policy networks trained via RL. Additionally, we analyze an application of this capability in transfer learning to diagnose and understand the decision-making processes of existing agents.

This study examines the $t$-$J$ model with nearest-neighbor hopping and spin exchange on the two-dimensional herringbone lattice. By adjusting the ratio of these interaction terms, we transition the system from an antiferromagnetic stripe phase to a superconductor with a gap exhibiting $d_{x^2-y^2}$ symmetry. Utilizing a combination of mean-field theory and $d$-wave boson mean-field theory, we analyze the resulting excitation spectra. Our findings indicate that applying a chemical potential shift or a uniaxial strain can modify the internal structure of the boson excitation gap. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both perturbations serve as effective strategies for achieving a doped hole-polaronic state characterized by an ultralow effective mass.

This study investigates risk-sensitive reinforcement learning within finite Markov decision processes, aiming to determine if the average restarts employed by this approach can enhance the overall risk-sensitive performance. The analysis demonstrates that, under appropriate conditions, there exist finite Markov decision processes where both the expected return and the expected risk-sensitive return remain well-defined, though maximizing expected return does not necessarily yield the highest expected risk-sensitive return. Additionally, the second law of large numbers applies equally to standard reinforcement learning and that of a risk-sensitive variant. By applying a Bernstein inequality to show that expected risk-sensitive returns fluctuate more than those of standard learning, the authors argue that the risk-sensitive return generally exhibits a higher level of stability compared to the standard expected return. Consequently, the findings indicate that restarting algorithms may indeed boost the risk-sensitive return, with the study providing a method to quantify this gain.

Distributed machine learning (DML) has become a focal point in both academic research and practical applications, gaining significant traction recently due to the rise of big data and the widespread adoption of deep learning. A primary goal of current DML research is to minimize communication costs, as bandwidth limitations often create bottlenecks for distributed systems. Recently, the weighted power-mean (WPM) aggregation function has emerged as a method to enhance convergence rates in distributed stochastic gradient descent (DPS), offering a non-linear alternative to the standard linear averaging used in most other aggregation schemes. This study investigates the impact of WPM on communication complexity within distributed optimization. We demonstrate that when WPM is combined with a linear unrolling strategy, communication complexity remains largely unaffected. Conversely, we find that applying a nonlinear inner-loop optimization using a nonlinear inner-loop (NNLL) approach with WPM substantially lowers communication requirements. Empirical results across multiple machine learning tasks confirm that this combination not only reduces communication frequency but also enhances model performance relative to conventional linear unrolling methods.

We introduce an optoelectronic device designed to convert radio-frequency signals into optical frequencies while maintaining synchronization with single atoms trapped in a cavity quantum electrodynamics (CQED) system. This approach holds promise for various quantum technologies, including the conditioning on atomic resonance for atomic responses, as well as in atom-based clocks and frequency comb systems.

This study introduces a valuated oriented graph formulation for the discrete mean curvature flow, demonstrating that it reduces to Edith Chung's specific model on valued trees when applicable. A novel concept of a "mean curvature flow" inside valuated oriented graphs is then defined. Subsequently, "zigzags" are introduced as tools to establish upper limits on closed upper sets of graph words, with the primary result providing specific estimates for graphs equipped with value assignments based on vertex degree.

Although the statistical mechanics of self-avoiding walks has guided the field of polymer physics for half a century, progress in understanding complex polymers with chemical memory—where the choice of the next monomer depends on the prior one—has been significantly slower. We introduce a new framework for analyzing these systems that represents each as a Markov chain of monomers with a defined state space. Using inference techniques from machine learning, we determine the minimal set of attributes required for individual monomers to accurately reproduce observed polymer distributions. Our data-driven approach is applied to extensive simulations of polymers featuring chemical memory, effectively modeling systems with as many as 20 distinct states. By achieving precise statistical accuracy with far fewer parameters than naive methods, our technique offers both high fidelity and computational efficiency.

This paper investigates the groups of deck transformations for the branched covering spaces associated with the dynamics of rational functions when considered as branched holomorphic maps. For any two bicritical rational functions whose post-critical sets have a rational function equivalence, the set of deck transformations for every common branched covering space forms a tower of finitely generated free groups. The authors establish that the growth of these free groups is governed by a linear fractionally recursive sequence. Furthermore, they demonstrate that the spectrum of the Laplacian for the corresponding covering spaces is purely absolutely continuous and exhibits a self-similar structure, a property that serves as necessary and sufficient for such recursive behavior of linear growth in such covering space dynamics for all braurally equivalent classes of maps.

This study examines a class of half-Cauchy prior induced by the scale-invariant prior on the precision matrix, which effectively approximates the g-prior on $\sigma^2$ when integrated marginally. We demonstrate that within an orthonormal basis, this prior system yields consistent and proper posterior distributions. Furthermore, we analyze posterior contraction rates in high-dimensional settings where the dimension $p$ exceeds the sample size $n$, specifically in the context of classical linear regression with $p > n$ and $p \to \infty$ while maintaining an error model with an unknown variance. Our findings indicate that accounting for variance uncertainty results in slower posterior contraction by a factor of $\sqrt{\log p}$. Additionally, we provide numerical evidence supporting our theoretical results.

This paper introduces a new approach to modeling machining processes, prioritizing the identification of key parameters and their specific impacts on critical quality characteristics. To achieve this, researchers employed the Taguchi method to design experiments, followed by Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and the Fuzzy Logic Inference System (FLIS) to examine how selected variables influence surface roughness. Experimental results indicate that feed rate is the dominant factor affecting surface roughness, with its fuzzy strength exceeding that of other variables by over 50%. Furthermore, a comparative assessment between a fuzzy inference system and a back-propagation artificial neural network (ANN) demonstrates that the FLIS outperforms the ANN in estimating surface roughness with greater accuracy.

We present a simple metric that defines a lower bound on the graph distance within finite, simple graphs that are connected and possess no self-loops or multiple edges between the same pair of vertices. The lower bound is determined by Ahlfors' constant, which represents the minimal possible Ahlfors regular conformal dimension among all metric spaces resulting from quotienting the graph's metric space using its first non-zero Laplacian eigenvalue. By estimating the upper bounds of this lower bound on specific classes of expanders, we derive simple formulas that constrain the growth of their graph distances.

This paper details our lattice QCD investigation of the hadron mixing parameter $\theta$ and $\theta'$ using the $N_f=2+1$ flavor sea quarks configuration provided by the Caltech/Stanford group. By employing an optimized variational method, we determine the mixing angle with the highest precision to date, achieving this through the most rigorous nonperturbative determination of the $Z_{\rm ren}$ renormalization constant available. Our analysis further explores hadronic properties, specifically the mass difference between the two states and the associated wave function renormalization constants.

This study evaluates how the unique characteristics of signatures—specifically distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability—influence the efficacy of automatic forgery detection systems. Using two large-scale signature datasets containing authentic and forged samples, the authors developed a new set of features to detect forgeries. These features leverage the relative complexity and variability of signatures, modeled through two new concepts: Local Signature Complexity (LSC) and Local Signature Variability (LSV). The study also examines how these metrics perform across signatures collected from both "naive" forgers and sophisticated professionals. Results indicate a strong correlation between the proposed features' performance and the distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of the signatures, offering significant insights for both automatic forgeries detection research and signature analysis.

We perform an analysis of how supersymmetry constraints within string theory dictate low-energy effective couplings. Our approach involves identifying suitable coupling terms in string theory that correspond to higher-derivative interactions in eleven-dimensional supergravity. We evaluate low-energy limits for Dp-branes and M-branes, determining their dependencies on massless couplings. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these determined relationships in the context of M-fift compactified on $S^6$, $T^6$, or Kähler manifolds yielding eleven-dimensional effective supergravity.

We investigate how temperature influences connected higher-order correlation functions within homogeneous, stationary many-body quantum systems. Our findings demonstrate that, unlike what might be expected, thermal fluctuations have a significantly reduced impact on these higher-order quantities compared to their counterparts at the level of second-order correlations. Leveraging the framework of weakly interacting bosons, we derive explicit analytical formulas for these connected correlations, beginning with the second order and extending through any order. These derived expressions reveal a striking characteristic: such temperature-dependent connected correlation functions are substantially smaller in magnitude compared to their zero-temperature equivalents. Furthermore, within the context of weakly interacting bosons at low densities and temperatures, we establish a rigorous mapping between these higher-order thermal correlations and specific joint probability distributions involving first- and second-order scattering processes. This connection facilitates a direct comparison between finite-temperature dynamics and zero-temperature collision events. Consequently, we argue that connected higher-order correlations play a diminished role in describing transport and many-body Dynamical processes when contrasted with second-order correlation functions.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the [N/ O] versus [ O/H] relationship in the Milky Way's disk, utilizing a chemical evolution model that accounts for both primary and secondary nitrogen production. By fitting a two-phase model to observed [ O/H ] gradients across the Galaxy's radial extent, we derive the [ N/ O ] evolution at a specific oxygen abundance level ([ O/H ] = -0.74), yielding a value of 0.65 ± 0.05 for early epochs and 0.97 ± 0.03 for later times. When primary N is assumed to arise from wind outflows of massive stars, our model successfully reproduces the [ N/ O ] trend observed in the solar system. Furthermore, we investigate the [ N/ O ] vs. [ O/H ] evolution within high-redshift damped Lyman-alpha systems (DLAs), finding a comparable evolution pattern to that of the Milky Way. However, the absolute [ N/ O ] ratios in these early-universe systems are marginally lower than those found in our Galaxy.

Research in Natural Language Processing (NLP) has historically prioritized English, largely due to the vast availability of high-quality resources. However, advances in deep learning and the lowering of computational barriers have enabled greater inclusivity, prompting a shift toward supporting diverse languages. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of multilingual NLP applications, highlighting their real-world applications and current challenges. We begin by outlining the evolving landscape of the field, hailing from the dominance of English to the rising prominence of resource-scarer languages. The core of our survey examines key application areas, including machine translation, semantic understanding, and generation. Additionally, we curated a collection of essential datasets and pre-trained models, organizing them by specific tasks to facilitate future research. We conclude by outlining promising avenues for ongoing investigation within multilingual NLP.

Integrating networked data and graph topology has emerged as a vital approach for analyzing complex biological systems. This integration enables researchers to leverage the rich informational content of biological samples to uncover the fundamental laws governing these intricate systems. This paper specifically examines the application of graph-based methods in understanding cardiac arrhythmias, a condition defined by irregular heart rhythms. We begin by reviewing the progress made in utilizing electrical and anatomical imaging data to characterize cardiac dynamics, followed by a discussion on the incorporation of these signals within increasing types of biological graph models.

The search for physics beyond the Standard Model frequently employs constraints derived from white dwarf (WD) observations. Within the Left-Right Symmetric Model, where a self-conjugate bi-doublet scalar couples to fermions, the new physics sector can be regulated by WD data. Our analysis begins with a WD density survey to establish a WD mass-radius relationship, enabling the determination of the central density. Assuming the core consists of neutrons and profs in beta equilibrium, we calculate neutrino loss rates due to the novel scalar interactions. By comparing these rates against observed WD thermal evolution, we derive limits applicable to the scalar couplings. Our findings indicate that WD observations impose tight constraints on the model's parameter space, particularly in the region of interest for electroweak symmetry breaking and parity restoration.

Recent studies have explored using graph models to analyze images while preserving privacy. We introduce the Graph Privacy Advisor, which enhances these traditional models by leveraging an image's metadata alongside its visual features. Evaluated on the private-photos dataset, our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art results. Additionally, we examine the outcomes to identify the specific characteristics that define photographs containing people or those that belong to photos with the main subject as a child.

This paper examines the influence of quantum-statistical entanglement on the entropy dynamics associated with radiation. The analysis focuses on two specific configurations: (1) the near-field radiation of a stochastically driven two-level atom, and (2) the quantum-statistical properties of radiation emitted by a moving two-level atom. The findings indicate that, in both cases, the entanglement between the two-level system and the radiation modes significantly alters the entropy behavior of the emitted field. Specifically, the entropic evolution in scenario (1) mirrors that of a moving atom in scenario (2) under corresponding conditions. Consequently, the motion-induced modification of the radiation's entropy characteristics can be interpreted as a direct result of the coupling between the atom and the surrounding radiation.

The LHC's central lead-lead (Pb+Pb) collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 2.76$ TeV were analyzed to investigate jet modifications accompanied by a high-$p_{\rm T}$ isolated photon. Measured in 2012, the data compare photon-tagged jets and inclusive jets against minimum-bias events, with the jet's transverse momentum relative to the photon ($p_{\rm T}^{\parallel}$) ranging from approximately 10 to 100 GeV and the photon's transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}^{\gamma}$) exceeding 100 GeV. The analysis reveals distinct differences in the $p_{\rm T}^{\parallel}$ spectra for central collisions versus minimum-bias events: the yield of high-$p_{\rm T}^{\parallel}$ jets is suppressed, whereas the yield of low-$p_{\rm T}^{\parallel}$ jets is enhanced. These findings indicate that high-$p_{\rm T}$ isolated photons serve as effective agents to probe jet modifications within the quark-gluon plasma.

Building upon the findings of our previous research, this paper introduces a robust approach for solving contact problems in rigid body dynamics. This introduction also details a new simulation of a 2D version of "Beamish," a classic two-dimensional gravity game. We propose leveraging this game not only to demonstrate the efficacy of our model but also to establish it as a valuable benchmark for comparing computational performance. Anticipating the widespread availability of future hardware capable processing low-precision values, our comparisons utilize both 32-bit and 16-bit floating-point variants, offering specific insights into how reducing precision impacts simulation speed.

Despite the known prevalence of nanoflare activity on the Sun, detecting hard X-ray (HXR) radiation from these areas remains challenging due to the instrument's limited exposure duration and the dominance of Earth's background noise. We describe the SXR and particle detectors, the SXR imaging technique, and the SXR image reconstruction algorithm. Predicting user influence in expansive social networks is a critical challenge with far-reaching applications. Although recent studies suggest that data augmentation can enhance the accuracy of this prediction, they are limited to small-scale datasets. This work investigates whether time and spatial augmentation techniques remain effective for influencing prediction tasks within large graphs. Through experiments on two substantial real-world datasets, we find that while augmentation initially boosts Node2Vec-based influence prediction performance on a smaller network, these gains vanish when the methods are applied to a larger dataset. Additionally, we introduce a novel augmentation strategy for influence prediction, which we prove is ineffective. Based on these findings, we conclude that temporal and spatial augmentations likely improve performance only by helping overcome overfitting in networks characterized by smaller sizes. Finally, we propose a robust Node2Vec-based model, validated through rigorous testing, that successfully generalizes to identify user influence across two large-scale social graphs.

Optimization methods within quantum field theory (QFT) are frequently linked to Euluer-Arnold equations defined on Lie groups. This study demonstrates that incorporating Euluer-Arnold equations directly into a backpropagation framework facilitates the construction of an effective quantitative annealing algorithm for a specific optimization task in QFT. By integrating these dynamics, we derive an annealing protocol governed by the Euluer-Arnold equations on the Grassmannian group. Furthermore, Euluer-Arnold equations serve to characterize the stationary points reached by this optimization process. The proposed numerical annealing method is validated through applications in supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory and the Dirac-Born-Infeld action.

This work addresses sensor calibration for pose estimation by incorporating more extensive internal sensor state information into the errors-in-state formulation. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on generic white noise models for sensor correlations, this study utilizes the sensor's internal state to capture complex, non-stationary, and time-coupled correlation structures. By relying on readily available data, this method enhances the generality of calibration models and leverages it fully within errors-in-state framework. Furthermore, this approach integrates more generic models into the errors-in-state framework without compromising computational efficiency or scalability. Finally, the proposed technique allows for the use of standard state-estimation tools, such as the Kalman filter, to execute these more rigorous calibration procedures.

This study introduces the idea of a multi-temperature universe to examine how the dark matter cross section varies across different scales. By extending the standard cosmological model with several distinct matter components, we formulate a multi-branch Hubble parameter that enables the derivation of corresponding multi-branch equations of state for dark energy and the Higgs field. These findings indicate that the dark matter cross section is not uniform; it is no longer considered a constant throughout all scales.

This document presents a study of the production of same-sign W boson pairs at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV utilizing proton-proton collision data from the LHC, with a total integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ gathered by the ATLAS detector. Within the high-$\beta_T$ region of same-sign WW pairs, an observed significance of 4.1 standard deviations (sigma) is noted above Standard Model predictions, which stands in contrast to a 3.9 sigma significance calculated relative to a Standard Model background-only hypothesis. Additionally, differential cross-sections are presented as functions of the transverse mass of the WW pair, the transverse mass of the lepton-neutrino system for each side, the transverse momentum of each lepton, the rapidity of the boson pairs, and the scalar sum of the transverse momenta of all final-state objects.

We propose an end-to-end trainable method for full control over the details of RGB colorization through a new variational formulation. This is achieved by extending the concept of the normalizing flow to a functional level, enabling likelihood maximization over functions. Our specific approach, the Colorization Normalizing Flow over Image Space (CNF-OI), demonstrates superior performance compared to our baseline CNN-based model (CNP-OI) and existing colorization techniques like API and CycleColor. Additionally, our framework supports various adaptations for different tasks, ranging from standard colorization and demosaicking to stain and tone transfer, all while maintaining effective color information.

This study examines the $P(q)$ model, a framework describing a flat universe containing dark energy, dark matter, and radiation, within a Bayesian analysis of the latest Planck 2018 data. We explore both flat and non-flat variations of the model, incorporating the Alcock-Bocuse ($A_L$) parameter to constrain curvature. Additionally, we integrate Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) data to further restrict cosmological parameters. Our investigation considers two scenarios: one fixing the amplitude of the primordial scalar fluctuations to the Planck 2018 best-fit value ($A_L=1$) and another allowing it to vary freely. When analyzing the non-flat model with a fixed amplitude ($A_L=1$), our results indicate that the original Planck $P(q)$ formulation yields significantly tighter constraints on cosmological parameters compared to the new extended model.

In collaborative coding environments, shared files serve as essential resources for teams, yet the maintenance practices of these files often vary significantly. This study examines how projects maintain shared objects by analyzing 1,102 GitHub repositories to quantify the extent of maintenance performed. Findings reveal that the maintenance effort per shared file is not uniform; it differs substantially across repository types and projects. The study further identifies specific factors that explain these differences and offers recommendations to aid developers in making more informed decisions regarding shared file maintenance.

Our analysis incorporated high-resolution spectra from the CORALIE and HARPS spectrographs, alongside photometric data from the TESS, CoRoT, and BRITE missions. The primary objective was to determine the physical parameters of both stars and search for potential third light contributions. Corroborating previous findings, our confirmation of the dual-pulsation nature of the system involved identifying radial velocity variations and analyzing pulsation frequencies. To address the challenges of sparse and noisy user behavior data, this study introduces a novel framework for aspect-based user preference learning in recommendations. At its core lies the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, which is designed to capture, refine, and aggregate a user's distinct preference patterns. Concurrently, to leverage auxiliary information from related aspects, the system employs cross-domain user preference transfer through a contrastive learning approach. Additionally, the framework integrates a loss function tailored for recommendation tasks. Extensive experiments conducted on three aspects of a comprehensive dataset demonstrate that the proposed system, named AULN, consistently surpasses existing baseline methodologies.

We utilize standard obstruction theory within the framework of Duffour and Nakai to analyze it on the space of $E_2$-algebra structures defined by the Chevalley-Eilenberg complex associated with the pair $(\pi, S)$, denoted as $[\pi, S]$. This analysis is applied specifically to sheaves of symplectic manifolds, where the E$_2$-algebra structure is constructed from the first relative symplectic cohomology of the sheaf. Consequently, there exists a spectral sequence originating from the E$_2$-algebra formed by the first symplectic cohomology of the sheaf and converging to the symplectic cohomology of the sheaf relative to $[\pi, S]$. Using this result, we obtain an algebraic framework for the E$_2$-algebra structure of the relative symplectic cohomology, analogous to the known structure for the relative symplectic cohomology of a manifold with boundary. Further, we apply these findings to establish the existence of a smearing map originating from the E$_2$-algebra of the relative symplectic cohomology and terminating in the E$_2$-algebra of the relative symplectic cohomology of the sheaf relative to $[\pi, S]$.

We introduce a stable, exact, and optimal method for least squares function approximation given a set of precise data points. While weighted least squares ensures first-order optimality across all function spaces when exact data points are used, it historically lacked a stability guarantee due to the non-constructive nature of a required positive-definite weighting matrix. Resolving this issue, we employ the singular value decomposition to create the proposed algorithm. It utilizes an eigenvalue-eigenfunction expansion over the space of the input features to ensure both exactness and stability, while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to that of simple least squares.

The hadronic interaction X(3872)+Z → D⁰ D⁰ and X(3872)+Z → D⁰ D⁰ has been investigated using a HBT analysis of non-identical protons to explore the internal structure of the X(3872)+Z particle. The reaction's cross-sections were calculated using the flux tube model, considering the X(3872)+Z as a bound state of D⁰ and D⁰. The non-identical proton pair production rate was analyzed to examine how the X(3872)+Z's configuration, binding energy, and the distance between the produced D⁰ and D⁰ affect the outcome. The results indicate that the non-identical proton pair production rate is highly sensitive to the X(3872)+Z's internal structure and the separation of the D⁰ and D⁰. The study also investigates how the QGP's HBT radii, shear viscosity, and the deconfinement transition's deconfinement radius influence the final hadronization process. The analysis suggests that the non-identical proton pair production rate can be used to constrain the QGP's HBT radii and the deconfinement transition's deconfinement radius, as well as to test the QGP's shear viscosity. Building on the work of Gelfand and Sottile, we establish exchange rules for a broadened version of the standard Osgood (OGS) framework tied to the bN Coxeter group $B_n$. These exchange laws maintain relationships with Coxeter length and descent position, mirroring the properties of the original system for the groups $B_n$.

This paper investigates the correlation functions for $O(N)$-symmetric, interacting, and non-relativistic bosonic field theories in $d=1$ spatial dimension ($v=1$). Beginning with the effective action and its associated Schwinger-Dyson equations, we derive expressions for correlation functions involving up to four scalar fields. We specifically examine how explicit symmetry breaking terms impact these calculations and demonstrate that such breaking results in the non-conservation of the $U(1)$ current. Our findings indicate that the associated correlation functions can effectively be computed by utilizing a relaxed, symmetry-breaking effective action.

This paper presents a methodology for robot acquisition of manipulation skills within unpredictable real-world settings. The process begins with robot demonstrations, where the unknown task is represented as a probabilistic selection from a predefined library of candidate tasks. A hierarchical Bayesian model is employed to estimate a task's posterior belief, enabling data acquisition strategies that rapidly adapt to new situations by leveraging similarities with past observations. Consequently, this approach allows demonstrated data to be shared across various elements of an task, such as the robot itself, environment, or object types, providing statistical leverage on data confounders that typically hinder real-world learning. We validate this framework through a robot stacking simulation, comparing it against a standard maximum likelihood baseline. The results confirm that our method successfully learns entirely novel tasks using significantly less data than the baseline, demonstrating its robustness in handling the variability inherent in real-life manipulation.

Let $G$ be a discrete group and let $X$ be a connected CW-complex with fundamental group $G$. The cover $\tilde{X}_H$ corresponding to a subgroup $H \le G$ can be equipped with either the whisker topology or the lasso topology, both of which yield a space that is either simply a subset of the universal cover $\tilde{X}$ or a quotient thereof, each endowing $\tilde{X}_H$ with a topological structure. In this work, we examine the relationships among these whisker, lasso, and the standard topologies within $\tilde{X}_H$. Specifically, we prove that the whisker and lasso topologies always agree on $\tildeX_{H}$ if and only that the index $[G:H]$ is finite. Additionally, we provide a counterexample demonstrating a scenario where the lasso topology differs from the standard topology on $\tildeX_{H}$. Finally, we determine precisely when the lasso topologized $\tilX_{H}$ is simply connected.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has proven effective for robot motion planning, but its slow learning rates necessitate millions of trials to achieve competent performance. This study introduces a new DRL framework for autonomous vehicle motion planning that leverages pre-trained models from other DRL agents. By utilizing these approaches, the motion planning phase can be re-conceptualized as an offline reinforcement learning task utilizing the stored trajectories. This methodology allows for direct application to motion planning without requiring further modifications to the original algorithms. Experiments conducted in a traffic scenario, which involved navigating alongside other vehicles, demonstrated that using these techniques significantly accelerates the learning process for DRL.

We investigate the growth of massive black holes in early galaxies, focusing on the role of unstable accretion disks. By modeling the formation of these disks via an Eddington-type gas model, we find that the disk's mass builds up to approximately $10^5$ times the central black hole's mass over a typical star-formation timescale. Consequently, the resulting black hole mass is a fraction of the star-formation timescale divided by the free-fall time at the black hole, multiplied by the initial black hole mass. This accretion also generates a strong outflow, which expels gas from the galactic center and suppresses star formation within the inner regions. This outflow-driven suppression may explain the observed flat slopes in the black hole mass–stellar mass correlation for inner galaxies. Additionally, we demonstrate that the ratio of a black hole's mass to its star-formation timescale remains constant throughout the growth process, regardless of the initial conditions.

Training deep learning models to perform reliable classification is essential for real-world deployment. In this study, we investigate how uncertainty quantification can enhance the performance of our RNN-based deep learning models. We find that by employing test-time augmentation alongside deep learning ensembles for prediction, results are improved. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in this area by achieving a 1.5% increase in accuracy over existing methods. We also observe a significant 1.4% increase in accuracy by utilizing an uncertainty-aware model updating strategy during inference. This approach enables us to correct misclassified samples and improve the overall model robustness. Our method is particularly effective for scenarios where the RNN model has been trained to use a soft-max classifier for prediction. We also note that our uncertainty-aware model updating strategy can be applied to any deep learning model that has been trained to use a classifier for prediction.
