This work introduces a new algorithm called Bonsai that facilitates human-in-the-loop (HILO) feature engineering within machine learning. It constructs a tree-structured space of features by iteratively refining the topology of the tree and learning associated local local representations. These features are generated by integrating human feedback into automatic learning processes, enhancing both feature quality and model performance. Specifically, users can guide Bonsai by providing feedback on how certain comparisons between data points should influence feature values. Experiments conducted on both real-world datasets and synthetic examples demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy.

Achieving high resolution and contrast when imaging through scattering media is crucial for numerous applications, yet it remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce a Weighted-Mutation Assisted Genetic Algorithm (WEGA) capable of reconstructing the original object from a scattered image by reversing the scattering process. In this framework, the genetic algorithm manipulates a binary matrix representing the object, where a pixel is either active (1) or inactive (0). A discrepancy metric is calculated to measure the difference between the current generated image and the target scattered pattern; the goal is to minimize this metric through an iterative evolutionary process. While a standard genetic algorithm relies on random mutation, we enhanced this process using WEGA, which increases the likelihood of mutating pixels corresponding to prominent (heavy) objects within the scene. By prioritizing significant features, WEGA accelerates convergence toward the optimal solution, resulting in superior image reconstruction performance, higher speed, and improved minimization of the discrepancy metric compared to conventional approaches.

We then estimate the average of these features across different policies, weighted by the covariance of their features. Monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensors are being increasingly favored for medical imaging applications. These devices are typically fabricated with thin layers, resulting in a charge-collection region that extends significantly beyond the sensor. This structural characteristic introduces a mismatch between the charge generation volume and charge collection volume, which can distort the charge-sharing profile. This study presents an analytical examination of how sensor thickness influences charge-collection profiles in monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensors. The findings indicate that the charge-sharing profile is markedly sensitive to the charge-collection layer thickness. Specifically, increasing the thickness of the electron-drift layer causes a pronounced reduction in charge-sharing probability at low energies. The study further quantifies the relationship between charge-generation and charge-collection properties as a function of incident photon energy.

We introduce a new direct imaging technique for exoplanets using image deconvolution, specifically tailored for ground-based observables limited by atmospheric turbulence. This method, called Deconvolution on Planets by AnLyzing Rotations (PLANR-DCSE), leverages the natural rotational symmetry of stellar systems to separate faint planetary signals from the glare of the host star. By analyzing images at various rotation angles, the approach suppresses symmetric noise patterns to reveal objects hidden within the stellar halo. We implemented the method using the Adaptive Optics imager at the Gran Telescopio Canarias (AO-Telescopio Gran Canarias) on the 10.4-meter telescope. The results demonstrate the successful detection of a planet orbiting the M-dwarf star 2MASS J22282881-4647393, an object previously undetected by direct imaging methods. The planet's separation of 0.21 arcseconds and magnitude difference of 4.2 from its host star mark the smallest contrast ratio achieved to date using image deconvolution. Furthermore, we provide an analysis of the method's performance, including its ability to resolve this contrast limit and the extent to which it remains robust against residual image artifacts.

This study introduces a new modeling approach for a macroeconomic system that simultaneously addresses negative interest rates and the phenomenon of demand for cash under such conditions. The model's analytical foundation utilizes the Carak and Rios-Rull (CRR) framework, enhanced by the inclusion of a search-theoretic cash holding model capable of functioning alongside a negative real interest rate. Research indicates that a significantly larger portion of economic agents hold cash when interest rates decline to zero or become negative. Furthermore, a new numerical simulation method is developed to solve the system of differential equations, which can be applied to both standard positive interest rate environments and those accommodating negative rates. When analyzing the impact of stochastic technology shocks within a two-sector New Keynesian model featuring a linearized New Keynesian IS curve, the findings demonstrate that the presence of an option to hold cash amplifies the magnitude of output fluctuations.

The community-driven design of the DUNE Near Detector, as documented in this white paper, prioritizes capturing a comprehensive spectrum of physics objectives. The proposed design is deemed most suitable for addressing key scientific goals, particularly long-distance neutrino oscillations, while also supporting a broad range of additional experiments. The document details the Near Detector's architecture, including its layout, components, neutrino-target system, neutrino-detector media, data-acquisition system, and control infrastructure. The authors also explore how this design influences and impacts the Near Detector's efficacy in searching for sterile neutrinos.

This study introduces novel cluster-robust estimators designed for linear models featuring both cluster-specific intercepts and heteroskedastic variances. Unlike standard cluster-robust estimators, which rely on consistent cluster variance estimates, our approach is valid under cluster heteroskedasticity caused by idiosyncratic variances that vary independently within clusters. Simulations demonstrate that these estimators achieve better asymptotic normality and superior finite-sample performance, particularly in small samples with numerous clusters, compared to traditional cluster-robust methods. Additionally, the new estimators exhibit greater resilience to outliers and misspecified cluster structures. Finally, we present an easily implementable, general-purpose software tool that applies these estimation methods.

Incorporating particles into computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations frequently results in an inefficient scaling of traditional numerical integration schemes, which restricts the time-step size to that permitted by the most constrained dynamics within the system. This limitation severely restricts both the temporal resolution and overall computational performance. To address this imbalance, we introduce the Multiple-Time-Step Integration Algorithm (MTSA), designed to adaptively calculate time-marching steps for each physical component based on its specific dynamical behavior. By implementing this algorithm alongside the Large Eddy Simulation (LES) framework, we demonstrate that MTSA successfully scales simulations containing millions of particles across various CPU cores. Furthermore, when compared to conventional particle-laden LES approaches, our methodology achieves significant reductions in computational cost while preserving accuracy equivalent to standard single-time-step techniques.

This paper examines the concept of particle number within the context of a quantum scalar field interacting with gravity during the semiclassical stage of black hole formation and subsequent evaporation. We demonstrate that the process of Hawking radiation can be articulated as particles escaping the black hole because the definition of particle number inherently depends on time, meaning the evolving spacetime background renders vacuum states non-stationary. We further propose a framework to quantify particle number in this dynamic scenario, utilizing it as a foundation for analyzing information retention in black hole evaporation. Ultimately, our findings indicate that defining particle count in such settings offers crucial insights into how black holes retain information throughout their lifecycle.

This study investigates how variations in dipole cross-section models affect predictions for broadening in high-energy $p$-$A$ and $PB\text{-}\to \ d\text{jet}+\text{jet}$ collisions, evaluated through both analytical calculations and numerical simulations. We compare multiple dipole cross-section formulations, applying them to a $d\sigma\_T$ model that accounts for both transverse and longitudinal dimensions, assessing their predictive power for changing nuclear sizes and center-of-mass energies. Additionally, we analyze the sensitivity of this broadening to the transverse dimensions when using different dipole cross-sections. Finally, we present the first broadening predictions derived from both the Iancu-Musulmanov-Peskov-Salamov (IMPS) and Balitsky-Kovchegov (BK) evolution equations, utilizing a $d$-dependent dipole cross-section, and discuss these findings in the context of future experimental measurements.
For $n \ge 2$, let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $a^{n-1} + b^{n-1} = 7^n$. The objective is to find the maximum value of $a + b$.

A two-way air-water coupling model is developed to simulate the dynamics of a jet within an entrained air layer. This system features a narrow channel with a periodic expansion, where a liquid jet enters the constrictions and alternates between striking the walls and the air-water interface. By employing a level-set method, the interface is tracked, and the interface shear stress is calculated to determine the resulting air flow. The model's predictions were validated against experimental data, which showed strong agreement. The study examines how variations in the entrained air layer's thickness influence the system's periodic stability and the jet's impact forces. Furthermore, by varying flow rate and the air layer's properties, the researchers analyzed the resulting jet behavior and stress distributions. The findings indicate that a thicker entrained air layer enhances system stability by reducing peak impact stress, whereas higher air viscosity and lower surface tension can lead to unstable periodic responses.

Non-volatile memory (NVM) represents a significant advancement in computing, offering storage that retains data without power while enabling hardware closer integration with software. As applications increasingly adopt NVM, ensuring data consistency becomes a critical challenge. This paper presents a new, lightweight, and highly scalable software technique for maintaining data consistency by leveraging algorithm-derived knowledge. This knowledge, derived from a computing algorithm's logic, includes information about which memory locations depend on specific internal states and how these states evolve during execution. By utilizing this metadata, our approach allows an application to save only essential, consistency-critical data in NVM, thereby avoiding unnecessary overhead. We have developed a software library implementing this method, which operates with minimal impact on performance, incurs negligible overhead, and remains largely independent of system architecture or hardware specifics. Furthermore, we provide a CPU microarchitecture designed to leverage NVM capabilities, which has been validated through a comprehensive evaluation of real-world applications running on both NVM-enhanced systems and traditional volatile-storage systems.

The Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM) is a widely used Bayesian method designed to uncover latent structures within information networks by analyzing collections of documents. However, traditional statistical approaches often fail to capture the full content of documents, limiting HDTM's performance and interpretability. To address this limitation, we introduce a content-enhanced variant known as the Hierarchical Document Topic Model with Pseudo Words (HDTM-PW). This adaptation integrates a content-rich topic distribution into the standard HDTM framework through the use of Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). Specifically, LDA generates external topic structures from large datasets, yielding a set of topics that reflect actual document content rather than relying solely on probabilistic assumptions. These external topics function as "pseudo words" within HDTM-PW, thereby reducing network-level inference errors. We evaluate the model's performance using both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that HDTM-PW outperforms conventional Bayesian models in recovery accuracy. Furthermore, we illustrate the model's practical utility by applying it to analyze the structure of the Twitter network surrounding the 2016 U.S. Presidential election.

This study examines three-body systems initialized with randomly selected coordinates and momenta, focusing on the frequency of two-body escape events. We analyze specific parameters, including the statistical properties of the remaining non-escaper three-body systems and the temporal distribution of escape events when it occurs, comparing our findings with relevant three-body theories. We found that the statistical distributions of post-encounter state variables align well with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, when escape happens, the distribution of its timing approximates a log-normal curve. We also investigated three-body systems starting near zero-energy states, where two-body binding is likely. We discovered that the two-body bound/unbound state depends primarily on the sign of the two-body zero-energy parameter, largely independent of the sign associated with the other pair. Additionally, when the system energy is close to zero, the distribution of escape times follows an exponential law.

The ALICE collaboration at the LHC reported findings on the nuclear modification factor, $R_{AA}$, for prompt J/$\Psi$ mesons with a transverse momentum exceeding 2 GeV/c across various centralities at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. This study utilizes an updated data set to investigate the suppression of prompt $\psi(2S)$ mesons ($R_{AA}^{\psi(2S)}$) in proton-lead (p-Pb) collisions, employing the same analysis methodology. By applying this approach, we derive $R_{AA}^{\psi(2s)}$ in proton-proton (pp) collisions and subsequently calculate the double nuclear modification factor, $R_{AA}^{\mathrm{rel}}$, defined as the ratio of $R_{AA}^{\psi(2s)}$ to $R_{AA}^{\mathrm{rel}}$ in p-Pb to $R_{AA}^{\mathrm{rel}}$ in pp collisions within the same kinematic and centrality conditions. Our results indicate that prompt $\psi(2s)$ mesons exhibit significant suppression in p-Pb collisions, which is notably stronger than the suppression observed for prompt J/$\Psi$ mesons within the same transverse momentum spectrum. Furthermore, the magnitude of suppression for prompt $\psi(2s)$ mesons increases with collision centrality.

We present a new correspondence linking equivalence relations on non-standard sets within a semantic framework of continuous logic, specifically among the compact metric spaces that constitute the $C$-logic elementary extension class. This elementary class is organized as the full subcategory of the Efremovich–Bourbaki completion of those 0-types whose diameters are bounded by some $\delta > 0$. Focusing on the case where $\delta = \frac{1}{2}$, we analyze how equivalence classes map onto complete metric spaces and how their individual completions relate through maps of bounded Lipschitz constant. These findings pave the way for a more accessible, more "Bourbaki-style" understanding of key notions in first-order theory continuous logic.

This paper introduces a strategy for monitoring software evolution that utilizes the matrix's singular value decomposition (SVD) to isolate and manage noise. The evolution of a system is represented as a matrix, where entries correspond to the correlation coefficients between various program elements. The authors propose truncating smaller singular values to filter out noise, subsequently reconstructing the matrix through this process. The method is validated using empirical data from the BouncyCastle library, demonstrating its efficacy.

Deep sequential models, characterized by their recurrent nature, have proven effective in numerous applications ranging from language modeling to speech recognition. However, their efficacy is often hindered by long-term dependencies in data sequences, a challenge that has historically limited their performance. Although attention mechanisms have emerged as a popular solution for addressing these dependencies, their integration into recurrent neural networks (RNNs) remains controversial. This study offers a fresh perspective on applying attention to recurrent models, supported by comprehensive experiments on standard benchmarks for language modeling and machine translation. We present a straightforward yet highly effective architecture, which achieves state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, we analyze various attention mechanisms, including self-attention, to identify their specific advantages and disadvantages.

Cassiopeia A (Cas A) serves as a premier laboratory for investigating the magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) of supernova remnants. In this study, we present X-ray polarization measurements from the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) targeting Cas A. Our findings reveal that the polarization degree peaks at approximately 20% within the central region, declining toward the periphery, while the polarization angle maps the azimuthal angle in the plane perpendicular to the line of sight. This observed angle pattern aligns with the magnetic field orientations previously deduced from radio data, suggesting that X-ray synchrotron radiation from a turbulent shock front produces these observational characteristics. Furthermore, our data indicate a moderate dependence of the polarization degree on X-ray energy, with the effect being most pronounced in the South-West sector. Collectively, these results constrain the polarization fraction in synchrotron emission from turbulent shocks and offer valuable insights into the magnetic field structure surrounding the supernova's shock front.

The note demonstrates that for any $n$-element set with positive integers, requiring distinct subset sums only for subsets of size at most $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$ increases the minimum possible maximum element from $2^{n-1}$ to $3^{(n-1)/3}$.

This study examines the equation of state for quark stars, specifically analyzing how deconfinement phase transitions affect their properties. Our findings indicate that above the deconfinement temperature, quark stars transition into neutron star configurations. In contrast, below this temperature, they form hybrid stars. Our analysis demonstrates that the radius of these hybrid stars is notably smaller than that of neutron stars.

The paper introduces the compass state, a newly developed non-classical state for metrology, and investigates how its number variance influences the estimation of a damping parameter. We demonstrate that although the non-Gaussian compass state offers enhanced sensitivity for estimating dissipative parameters in open quantum systems, it does not offer an advantage over the Gaussian thermal state. We conclude by suggesting that for metrological purposes, the primary determinant of sensitivity is the number variance, which helps explain why thermal states are often preferred in practical applications.

We introduce a novel algorithm designed to characterize the geometry of particle tracks within jets produced by hadrons in particle collisions. This "Hadron Jet Classifier" (HJC) models the internal dynamics of color string fragmentation to distinguish between light quark and gluon jets. By leveraging light-cone fragmentation theory, the method analyzes light-cone momentum fractions carried by jet particles, light-cone invariant mass scales, and relative angles to compute likelihood-based templates for gluon and quark jets. When applied to Monte Carlo simulations, the algorithm achieves an impressive discrimination performance of 80% while maintaining 90% efficiency for signal jets. Furthermore, the template parameters are constructed to remain robust against changes in hadronization models, enabling a successful test of the algorithm's application with data from the CMS detector at the LHC.

This paper introduces a new concept in virology, shifting focus from traditional views on viruses to "viral surface metabolism," which examines how viruses generate surface components during their replication cycle. The proposed mechanism explains viral rolling entry as a form of endocytosis driven by a conformational change in the viral capsid, which generates the necessary work to pull the viral surface into the cell. Furthermore, by applying this framework, which views viruses as surface entities, we can better understand how infection occurs and how viruses evade the host's immune defenses. Ultimately, this perspective offers a new approach to viral entry and infection that could guide the development of innovative antiviral therapies.

Warp galaxies are a rare class of spiral systems defined by significant deviations in their stellar disks, with the majority exhibiting U-shaped structures caused by external tidal forces and the other group, known as S-shaped warps, presumed to result from internal dynamics. This study investigates the environmental contexts of both types to determine the validity of the external origin hypothesis for S-shaped warps. By analyzing data from the Galaxy Zoo project, we identified 1,041 spiral galaxies with prominent warps and collected corresponding data on their local surroundings, including the proximity and morphology of neighboring galaxies. Our findings indicate that the environmental factors influencing S-type galaxies differ significantly from those affecting U-type galaxies; specifically, S-type systems experience weaker tidal forces from nearby neighbors and reside in regions with lower galaxy density. Additionally, while U-type galaxies are often associated with interacting pairs, S-type systems show no increased likelihood of interaction with their neighbors. The data further reveal that S-type warped galaxies are more likely to be found near the centers of galaxy groups or clusters, whereas those with U-shaped warps are predominantly located on the periphery. These results support the conclusion that the majority of S-type warped galaxies arise primarily from internal dynamical processes rather than external environmental triggers.

We demonstrate that if gradient shrinking Ricci solitons satisfy a growth condition of $O(r^{\frac{2}{d}})$ for harmonic functions defined on the manifold for some exponent $d>0$, then these functions define no more than an $d$-dimensional structure; that is, the functions vary only within a genuine $d$-dimensional submanifold.

We introduce a general approach to locate chiral topological compounds by combining first-principles calculations with topological band structure analysis. We identify Rb$_x$K$_{1-x}$Bi$_4$ and Rb$_x$Cs$_{1-x}$Bi$_4$ as promising chiral topological candidates, initially classified as T-type and W-type single-band models, respectively. We further predict that Li$_x$Na$_{1-x}$Sb and Li$_x$K$_{1-x}$Sb will exhibit chiral topological band structures, specifically as U-type and V-type models. Our analysis reveals that the phase symmetry of these materials can be regulated by adjusting their doping levels. Specifically, Rb$_x$Bi$_4$ and Rb$_x$CsBi$_4$ are stable in cubic structures but can be stabilized in hexagonal forms via a second-order phase transition induced by band inversion. Additionally, we observe that doping can induce a transition from W-type to U-type symmetry in KRb and from U-type to V-type in RbCs. These findings offer valuable insights for discovering new topological materials and suggest that this methodology can be applied to other chemical systems.

Driven by the need for efficient and accurate modeling of thermal transport, this study examines Born effective charges (BECs) in the dynamic regime. Our findings reveal that in pristine (clean) conductors, the nonadiabatic contributions to BEE are negligible compared to adiabatic terms; consequently, adiabatic approximations remain valid for modeling transport in such materials. Conversely, for adiabatic insulators and semiconductors where impurities are present, the nonadiabatic terms dominate over the adiabatic counterparts. We have implemented a strategy to explicitly calculate these nonadiabatic BEE terms and applied it to three-dimensional black phosphorus, yielding a significant increase in the BEE magnitude along with a dependence on both the concentration and the nature of the dopants.

Fluctuating hydrodynamics (FH) is a cornerstone approach for modeling turbulence and numerical dissipations within that framework. This study examines how fluctuating hydrodynamics relates to the classical energy cascade concept. We find that the FH-derived dissipation rate aligns well with the dissipative dissipation observed in direct numerical simulations (DNS) of Navier-Stokes equations, suggesting that the DNS mechanism mirrors fluctuating hydrodynamics. Consequently, we argue that the fluctuating hydrodynamics framework offers a physically robust basis for understanding the turbulence dynamics and the observed DNS energy cascade.

We provide an overview of magnetoelectric coupling, beginning with Witten effect's characterization of electric charge polarization induced by magnetism within a wound flux. This introduction proceeds to examine the modern era of magnetoelectricity, beginning with the theoretical foundations of the Rashba effect and advancing to its experimental realization. Subsequently, the text explores magnetoelectric phenomena across diverse material systems, ranging from oxides to topological insulators and superconductors. The discussion further details the experimental methodologies used to probe these effects, including the use of circularly polarized light, terminated surfaces, and the application of external fields. The work concludes by surveying the current landscape and future prospects of the field, emphasizing ongoing efforts to explore and exploit magnetoelectricity for emerging technologies.

Diffusion can significantly accelerate dynamics within systems featuring delayed nonlinearities, as seen in chemical reactions. Such enhancements typically arise from feedback loops, where current state influences future evolution, which in turn amplifies the immediate impact through the return path. This study examines a case where the nonlinearity operates as a low-pass filter, producing an output smoother than its input. Results indicate that, similar to explosive growth seen in other contexts, this type of feedback can still generate significant acceleration, although the mechanism differs. Specifically, the system's effective dimensionality decreases, raising the frequency of visits to specific states and boosting transition probabilities between them.

This paper explores the connection between higher-order probabilistic programs under denotational semantics and operational semantics. While previous research has primarily focused on operational models for first-order programs, our work bridges the gap by supporting higher-order functions through a suitable adaptation of the probabilistic lambda calculus. This foundational element allows first-order results to be extended to higher-order contexts. Specifically, we present base cases suitable for extending existing operational semantic definitions to higher-order levels, thereby enabling a higher-order interpretation of previous semantic theorems.

This study introduces an advanced methodology for designing effective strategies in code and documentation analysis to enhance design mining. Specifically, the proposed document approach refines traditional static extraction by leveraging both textual and structural properties through a hybrid design conclusion framework. Simultaneously, the proposed recommendation system refines design suggestion techniques by integrating both local and global context from an expanded design conclusion repository, thereby stabilizing results across different projects and improving their cross-project relevance. Empirical evaluations using a large-scale dataset of 100k+ Python functions demonstrate that the proposed document system outperforms existing designs in consistency, while the recommended structure achieves superior accuracy in design suggestion tasks.

The primary goal of this study is to demonstrate that the de Sitter horizon in the framework of future holographic dark energy (F-HDE) serves as a viable candidate for the negative-pressure dark vacuum energy responsible for the current accelerated expansion of the universe. We examine the evolution of the F-HDE equation of state (EOS) across various infrared (IR) cutoffs to determine which scenarios most accurately reflect the observed cosmic history. Our analysis indicates that the scenario proposed by Li et al., utilizing the F-HDE model with a specific particle horizon as the IR cutoff, offers the most realistic description of the universe's evolution. Furthermore, we calculate key physical parameters, including the F-HDE EOS, equation state parameter difference, and Brans-Dicke parameter, to evaluate the model's consistency with observational data.

We introduce a framework designed to identify collections of manifolds on which a function maintains differentiability, even when the underlying data function exhibits discontinuities in its first derivative. Within the context of black-box function representation, we demonstrate that an exact approximation of these differentiability manifolds can guide the search process by enforcing steps sufficient for infinitesimal change while ensuring gradient evaluations remain computationally feasible. Furthermore, we establish that when an algorithm exploits this identified structure, its convergence rate improves significantly compared to structure-agnostic approaches. Leveraging these principles, we developed a hybrid optimization method capable of navigating noisy, non-smooth landscapes by computing gradients efficiently.

Let $R$ denote an associative ring with identity. An ideal $P$ within $R$ is termed a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal if it is not a prime ideal, is not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal, and satisfies the property that for any three elements $a, b, c \in R$, the product $abc$ belonging to $P^2$ implies that at least one of the products $ab$, $bc$, or $ac$ belongs to $P$ (note: $a$ appears twice in the standard definition logic $a,b,c \to ab, bc, ac$). In this work, we establish that the cube of any such weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal, excluding its $1$-absorbing prime counterparts, yields an irredundant primary decomposition consisting of exactly two primary ideals.

The newly developed Time-Delayed Autoencoder (TDA) algorithm effectively uncovers the non-stationary, non-linear relationships between time series that auto-correlate. Its measured correlation lag offers practical utility in astrophysics, particularly for inferring the physical separation between interacting components in variable systems. When applied to the measured light curves of the micro-lensed quasar OJ 287, the TDA model demonstrates significant non-linear links between its emission lines. Specifically, the analysis reveals a two-year orbital period for the binary black hole system comprising OJ 287, aligning with prior research, and identifies an estimated black hole mass of approximately $8 \times 10^9$ solar masses.

Relational models in pharmacology have recently gained traction for their ability to incorporate structured knowledge and deliver explainable predictions. However, integrating complex knowledge graphs into these models presents significant hurdles, particularly regarding how graphs are represented and which performance metrics are appropriate for evaluation. This study introduces a new suite of benchmarks for comparing relational learning models in pharmacology, offering a more realistic assessment of real-world tasks. We offer clear guidelines on constructing appropriate benchmarks, including specific examples such as predicting drug-target interactions and synthesizing new drugs with customized profiles. By providing actionable recommendations for both benchmark creation and the selection of evaluation metrics, this work offers a roadmap for enhancing future developments in pharmacological relational learning.

This paper introduces an affordable, smartphone-based method for assessing road conditions, designed to overcome the limitations of traditional monitoring systems that rely on sparse, fixed sensors. Our approach leverages a smartphone application to gather data from users, effectively creating a dense, crowdsourced network of road quality evaluations. By processing this data through a machine learning model, the system generates a detailed road condition map. The system's validity was tested across the United States and across India, the United Kingdom, and the United United Arab Emirates. Results demonstrate a significant correlation between predicted classifications and actual measurements taken by professional vehicles, confirming the method's accuracy. Furthermore, the study investigates the influence of network size, data size, and the demographic and usage profiles of the crowd on monitoring outcomes.

Imitation learning is a highly effective approach for acquiring new skills by observing demonstrations. Nevertheless, even minor variations between the agent's internal simulation and the actual task setup can lead to drastic performance declines. To address this issue, we introduce a self-supervised strategy for on-policy data filtering that aligns the expert and learner environments through the removal of inconsistent state-action pairs. Our method operates by training a conditional state embedding network to compress state representations; simultaneously, a classifier attempts to distinguish whether these compressed features originate from the learner or the expert data streams. Consequently, samples classified by the learner are identified as dissimilar and excluded. Experiments across three distinct tasks demonstrate that this proposed approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in bridging substantial domain gaps. Additionally, we analyze the latent features and support vectors to provide insights into the internal mechanisms driving this process. The project's code and trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/ysj1999/EnvironmentAlignment.

The collapse of a rotating molecular cloud core initiates the formation of a protostar and an accretion disk. During this evolutionary process, angular momentum is transferred from the disk to the forming star via the star's magnetic field, which launches a magnetocentrifugal wind that ejects material from the system. This study examines the conditions under which this magnetocollapse-induced disk wind can trigger disk fragmentation, leading to the creation of multiple protostars. We find that such wind-induced fragmentation is possible if the magnetic field strength is sufficiently intense, a scenario that aligns with recent observations. However, the resulting binary or multiple star systems would have significantly lower angular momenta compared to those formed through standard accretion-enhanced collapse. Consequently, the orbits of the binaries would be much tighter, a distinction that could potentially differentiate these magnetically formed binaries from those born via direct accretion.

Association rules serve as a fundamental method for uncovering relationships among items in large datasets. However, standard mining techniques typically generate an overwhelming quantity of such rules, necessitating the elimination of unnecessary ones through filtering or post-processing. This work addresses the redundancy inherent in these rules by interpreting it as the consequence of logical entailment. We characterize redundancy using three equivalent definitions and demonstrate this understanding both theoretically and practically via the visualization of rule implications as a directed graph. Furthermore, by integrating our insights with existing knowledge, we frame the challenge of identifying and removing superfluous rules as one of Maximum Subgraph Identification involving transitive reduction within graph theory.

This study investigates crime recidivism patterns among individuals released from prison in New York City between 2009 and 2014, focusing on the influence of mental health treatment. The analysis reveals that, on average, treated offenders committed fewer crimes post-release than those who received no treatment; specifically, their offenses were more likely to be non-criimes. The evidence indicates that treatment effectively reduces recidivism, with the greatest impact observed among those treated for violent crimes, suggesting treatment successfully mitigates violence. Furthermore, although treatment does not significantly alter employment outcomes, it enhances educational attainment. These findings suggest that mental health treatment serves as a cost-effective strategy that improves both mental well-being and community safety.

This paper investigates Ackerberg-Villars type identities, Stirling numbers, and various polynomial families by deriving them through the square of a square-root of a binomial coefficient. The approach is primarily based on the utility of generating functions. Several of these results have been generalized, and it is observed that they encompass numerous known combinatorial formulas as particular instances.

This paper introduces an unsupervised deep learning approach for estimating radio maps, where a user-generated uncertainty metric for the map guides an adaptive policy to optimize the first-stage measurement gathering required for map creation. An approximate actor-crol algorithm is employed to optimize the resulting approximate decision value function, which utilizes a mapper to learn features relevant to the decision-making process. The authors validate the approach using a simulated dataset and compare it against methods employing random or uncertainty-based-only measurement selection, demonstrating that the proposed method yields superior radio map estimates.

Anomaly detection is a critical area of research with wide-ranging applications, including intrusion detection, fault diagnosis, and disease identification. While supervised learning approaches rely on labeled data to train models, obtaining such labels is often costly or impossible in real-world scenarios. In contrast, unsupervised methods identify deviations from normal patterns within unlabeled data, making them ideal for contexts where acquiring labels is unfeasible. This work introduces a deep learning framework for detecting anomalies using only unsupervised learning. The model employs an autoencoder to learn a compressed, efficient representation of the input data. Anomaly detection is then performed by analyzing the input-output reconstruction error generated by this network. The paper validates the approach's performance on two datasets: the KDDCup99 network intrusion dataset and a private set containing sensor data from a water treatment facility.

This paper introduces a new, lightweight verification system designed for short, noisy clear-text inputs, specifically targeting scenarios like text-to-text matching in chat applications where traditional similarity metrics fall short due to the constraints of noisy conditions and character-level granularity. The work evaluates three distinct approaches: two baseline methods (Edit Distance and Trigram Intersection over Union) and a binary classifier utilizing a Bidirectional LSTM with character-level input. The study also contrasts performance metrics, noting that while classifier accuracy reaches approximately 90% under ideal conditions, the base edit distance score drops to around 80% in clean text but significantly declines to roughly 60% when handling noisy inputs. The paper concludes that the proposed lightweight solution is best suited for its intended domain of cleaning short messages, whereas the edit distance approach remains more effective for general, clean-clear scenarios.

Data augmentation is a well-established method for enhancing classification systems, particularly in visual recognition, by artificially expanding datasets through transformations like rotation, translation, and color adjustments. This paper investigates how augmentation impacts classification performance in relation to the scale of the original training data. By analyzing both artificial and natural datasets, alongside various augmentation techniques, we observe that augmentation yields greater improvements on smaller datasets than on larger ones. Specifically, as dataset size increases, the performance gap between augmented and non-augulated models diminishes. These findings indicate that augmentation is most valuable for classifiers trained on limited data, offering strategic guidance for future research and practical applications.

This paper establishes conditions under which weak convergence in the space of continuous functions holds for empirical processes indexed by bounded measurable functions, specifically for nonparametric M-estimators. This framework encompasses maximum likelihood estimators and optimal fair estimators found in certain auction settings, as well as estimation tasks within U-processes. Once this weak convergence result is secured, it applies seamlessly to consistent and continuously differentiable (in the sense of Rockafellar and Stoica) $\theta \mapsto Q(\theta)$ functions defined on parameter spaces, where $Q$ takes values in a separable metric space. We further demonstrate the application of this theory by deriving weak convergence properties for the empirical processes associated with these estimates, including those in half-varying parameter models involving auctions and U-processes, as well as for maximum likelihood estimators within a specific class of nonparametric statistical models.

Privacy is paramount in data management systems, particularly those utilizing external data like search engines to augment internal repositories. Although numerous k-anonymity-based techniques exist for releasing such auxiliary information, they predominantly treat records as independent entities, overlooking the reality that data records often rely on mutual dependencies. These authors investigate how these dependencies influence privacy coverage within k-anonymity frameworks. They propose two novel k-anonymity protocols that incorporate the dependency structures of search engine data. The study evaluates the proposed methods by comparing their levels of privacy coverage, privacy risk, and computational efficiency against standard k-anonymity approaches.

This study investigates the effects of varying C/O ratios on chemical processes within protoplanetary disks, utilizing a new model that integrates the complex network of gas-phase reactions with dust grain chemistry. We demonstrate that reducing the C/O ratio leads to a significant decline in the disk column density of C$_2$H, a key molecule for tracing carbon-rich environments in these systems. This decline results from the formation of C$_2$H$_2$ and carbon clusters in the midplane, where gas-phase chemistry is governed by the dominance of carbon over oxygen. Additionally, we found that C$_2$H forms more readily in the upper, oxygen-rich layers of the disk, where UV photolysis of H$_2$CO and CH$_3$OH on dust grains produces abundant CH radicals that react with H$_2$. Our findings indicate that C$_2$H serves as a critical tracer for carbon-rich conditions in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, while the upper layers function as a sensitive indicator of the overall C/O ratio.

Scientific and technological advancements increasingly rely on the synchronization and temporal correlation of events across diverse time-scaled domains. While time-correlated data is ubiquitous in fields such as neuroscience, particle physics, and astronomy, the volume of these datasets is growing rapidly, necessitating robust and versatile tools for their examination. We introduce the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), a high-performance software solution capable of processing large-scale time-tagged information with superior speed and flexibility.

Unlike conventional approaches that often require prolonged processing times, ETA offers real-time capabilities, allowing for the immediate visualization of single events and statistical correlations. Its architecture supports flexible event filtering and the generation of both binned histograms and multidimensional parameter spaces. Furthermore, by supporting multiple proprietary and open formats, the ETA serves an expanding user base spanning physics, biology, and engineering sectors.

We present a solution to the mean field game framework where the regularity constraint is relaxed, allowing players' optimal trajectories to be absolutely continuous rather than requiring them to be differentiable. In this setting, the cost evaluation integrates over the time derivative of the trajectory for absolutely continuous paths, alongside spatial costs dependent on position and the magnitude of velocity. A key finding is that regularity conditions often hinder equilibrium existence; therefore, we demonstrate, under specific assumptions, the presence of L¹-equilibria. These findings can subsequently be extended to prove L²-equilibriums, which possess sufficient regularity such that the optimal strategies for both the mean field and individual players are smooth functions.

The hypothesis that the Milky Way's central black hole, Sagittarius A*, sustains an accretion disk composed primarily of stellar material allows for the reconstruction of the chemical and physical traits of infalling stars through the analysis of the black hole's own light. By applying the same methods used for standard stellar population studies, we can determine the age and composition of a "stellar string" surrounding Sgr A*. Our findings indicate that this population is remarkably homogeneous, likely due to the shared origin of these stars within a single cluster. Specifically, the stellar strings appear significantly younger than the group of local field stars situated nearby. Furthermore, the inferred chemical abundances align closely with observations of young open clusters within the Galaxy.

User-generated content in fashion, ranging from lookbooks to social media outfits, is abundant. However, manually identifying mismatching items within such collections is labor-intensive, a task made even harder by non-experts creating custom outfits on platforms like Pinterest and Polyvore. To address this, we introduce **FashionCheck**, a novel interface designed to detect inappropriately paired clothing in user-generated sets. This system employs an on-demand, controllable, and accurate image pairing detector that can either globally adjust entire collections or locally modify specific regions to correct mismatches.

The framework of resource theories has become a pivotal component in modern Inference and processing, particularly within the development of resource theories for quantum information processing. These theories are distinguished by their ability to provide a unified structure for formulating and solving problems related to quantum resource management. The following sections explore the fundamental structure of these theories, their applications in solving specific quantum information scenarios, and their potential to advance the field.

Federated learning (FL) represents a privacy-centric framework for collaborative machine learning, yet it struggles with scalability as issues with model accuracy persist due to heterogeneous client data distributions. The recently introduced Buff fed learning (BuffFed) algorithm addresses these hurdles by enhancing scalability and preserving privacy, though its reliance on storing encrypted updates in a central server limits further large-scale expansion. To overcome this constraint, we present a revised BuffFed algorithm that utilizes homomorphic encryption (HE) and multipartite computation (MPC) to perform aggregation computations directly on encrypted data without exposing it to the server. Our proposed HE-based MPC technique executes the calculation of federated model updates by operating entirely within the encrypted domain. Additionally, we develop an efficient implementation of this algorithm using the Paillie cryptosystem, which demonstrates substantial performance gains over existing He-based MPC approaches.

This work develops and examines the commutant of polynomial shift semigroups, which consist of $T_n f := f(n\cdot)$ for $n \ge 0$. A hierarchy of cal culi, each yielding distinct Calkan classes, is developed in order to build a single unified calculus, whose output precisely and completely represents the commutant itself.

We predict the direct detection rates for the galactic absorption of primordial black holes (PBHs) serving as all-dark-matter, utilizing the spin-dependent axial form factor recently derived for a proton target. This update builds upon our earlier work by incorporating these precise proton structure details. Our analysis targets the PBH mass window of 10^−21 to 10^−17 solar masses, where the resulting interaction cross-section is enhanced by significant momentum transfer scaling. Consequently, detection prospects are markedly improved in direct detection experiments employing Xenon, Krypton, or Argon isotopes. Even accounting for conservative estimates of the dark matter density provided by PBHs, our calculations reveal that current experimental sensitivities are poised to detect these events.

This work examines a particle raft situated within a thin, viscous fluid on a hydrophobic substrate, where particles self-propel by absorbing fluid and expanding, thereby generating pushing forces against one another. The collective pushing causes the raft to fragment into a series of rifts that function as hydrophobic channels. The analysis focuses on the dynamics of these hydrophobic channels, where the opposing processes of particle re-aggregation and raft expansion govern the spacing between rifts. By modeling the system as a non-linear dynamical one-dimensional map, we derive an expression for the distance separating adjacent rifts. The study identifies a threshold in particle number density beyond which the raft undergoes a transition to a periodic state of pulsation, characterized by a sudden expansion and rapid contraction. Finally, we contrast the theoretical predictions with experimental observations from particle rafts, confirming the model's validity.

Gallium nitride (GaN) is a leading material for high-power and high-frequency applications; however, its lattice mismatch with most III-V and II-VI compound semiconductures restricts epitaxial growth on substrates like Ge, Si, and ZnS. This limitation hinders the ability to leverage GaN's exceptional properties for creating novel heterostructures. This study investigates the lattice matching capabilities of ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiZn$_2$ with standard GaN crystal orientations. Utilizing first-principles density functional theory, we find that the [110] orientations of ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiZn$_2$ match the lattice constants of both 4H- and 6H-GaN with discrepancies under 0.2%. Furthermore, we analyze how this lattice matching influences electronic band structures and effective masses. We also estimate mobility enhancements in GaN at room temperature resulting from these perturbations, projecting increases of up to a factor of 100 for ZnGeN$_2$/GaN and 200 for MgSiZn$_2$/GaN heterostructures. Ultimately, these findings offer a pathway to novel GaN-based heterostructures that could significantly boost device performance.

This paper introduces a semi-parametric policy gradient strategy for policy iteration in autonomous navigation within underwater environments, implemented via the specific algorithm known as SPGP-SARSA. By integrating the advantages of both linear and nonlinear function approximators, SPGP-SARSA maintains the efficiency of policy evaluation associated with linear methods while retaining the flexibility of nonlinear approaches. We validate the algorithm's performance through comparisons with standard policy iteration using both linear and nonlinear approximators, demonstrating through simulations that it achieves faster convergence and superior final performance. Additionally, the algorithm's practical applicability is confirmed by deploying an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) to execute real-world maritime missions using maritime chart data.

This work derives new isothropic surfaces from simply connected patches by applying transformations such as isotropic Galilean transformations, isotropic translations, rotations, and isotropic Galilean rotations. These methods generate distinct isothermic surfaces characterized by different isothermic parameters, including isothermic surfaces of revolution, isotropic Galilean transformation surfaces, and related variants.

This paper presents a global stochastic collocation approach for solving parabolic partial differential equations featuring random coefficients. We employ a tensor product framework combining univariate grid points from independent variables with univariate nodes drawn from the independent collocation method. We then derive and analyze two methods to project the global scheme onto this tensor product grid. We perform a convergence analysis for these methods and demonstrate that they converge at nearly optimal rates. Furthermore, we compare these techniques against standard hierarchical algorithms based on Galerkin projections using kernel-based trigonometric basis functions through numerical experiments. The results indicate that our proposed global stochastic collocation methods offer superior approximation accuracy and convergence performance relative to these classical schemes.

This study introduces r-Gaussian and r-growing polynomials as r-analogs of Dowling polynomials within the framework of q-analogues. We establish their fundamental properties and demonstrate how they connect to various known combinatorial structures, including r-Bell numbers, r-Stirling numbers of the second kind, and multi-variable Bell numbers of both q-and q-analog forms as well as multi-variable extensions thereof. Furthermore, these applications extend to the q-and q-analog versions of these numerical sequences when the r-parameter is incorporated. Finally, we derive closed-form solutions for the q-and q-analog versions of these numerical sequences when the r-parameter is incorporated, showing how they connect to various known combinatorial structures, including r-Bell numbers, r-Stirling numbers of the second kind, and

Existing models for temporal knowledge graph embedding, such as TQE, have been outpaced recently by the simpler TKE time-embed approach. We propose a new method to further enhance temporal KG embeddings by utilizing an attention mechanism to dynamically weigh triplets, thereby improving performance on both link prediction and ranking tasks. We achieve this through Time-Attention KE (TAKE), which integrates temporal features more effectively than its predecessors. Experimental results demonstrate that TAKE surpasses current state-of-the-art models in efficiency and simplicity while delivering superior scores across benchmarks for both filtering and permutation ranking.

Let $G$ and $H$ denote graphs, and let $G^{in}$, $G^{out}$, $H^{in}$, and $H^{out}$ represent their respective in-split and out-split variants. We establish that $G^{out}$ is a graph related-by-conjugacy (strongly shift equivalent) to $G^{in}$ if and only if $G$ and $H$ possess related-by-conjugacy (strongly shift equivalent) in-split and out-split forms, respectively. Furthermore, considering graphs $G$ and $H$ that are already related-by-conjugacy (strongly shift equivalent), we determine that their in-split transformations ($G^{in}$ and $H^{in}$) are related-by-conjugacy (strongly shift equivalent) precisely when they share an equivalent related-by-conjugacy (strongly shift equivalent) out-split ($G^{out}$ and $H^{out}$).

By applying an anisotropic Stefan-Boltzmann scenario to long-range interactions, we ensure the proposed framework aligns with Stefan-Boltzmann scenario to the specific anisotropic lattice spacing. This paper proposes an anisotropic heavy-quark potential with a complex structure designed for non-covariant lattice spacings found in numerical simulations. Our framework incorporates heavy boson interactions characterized by an anisotropic Stefan-Boltzmann scenario applicable to long-range scales within such lattices.

This paper presents OREO-LM, a language model designed to address questions by integrating a multi-modal knowledge interaction layer with a multi-dialogue knowledge reasoning mechanism. In its architecture, this knowledge layer enables the incorporation of external resources, allowing the model to align linguistic input with knowledge graph (KG) structures for effective joint reasoning. Furthermore, a multi-conversational reasoning process is employed to sequentially engage Encyclopedic, Relation, and Ontology agents, each contributing distinct reasoning capabilities to the final output. Comprehensive evaluations on both knowledge graph interrogatives and natural language question-assessments demonstrate that OREO-LM achieves performance comparable to specialized multi-modal systems and significantly surpasses single-modal language models.

High dimensional expanders represent a generalization of expander graphs, emerging as a pivotal concept in theoretical computer science with promising applications ranging from sampling and derandomization to the analysis of message passing algorithms and their utility as a testbed for new ideas. This document provides an accessible introduction to the field, outlining the basics of high dimensional expandability and key research directions. Targeted at computer scientists seeking a overview and computer researchers interested in the concept, it also includes a concise appendix reviewing the necessary topology and algebraic tools.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently achieved remarkable success across numerous natural language processing tasks. Although these systems are highly versatile, their outputs are not guaranteed to be consistently reliable, particularly when processing inputs that diverge from their pre-training distribution. This limitation suggests that LLMs possess domain-specific capabilities rather than possessing truly general abilities. To investigate this boundary, we conducted an analysis using a suite of 2000 domain-agnostic, randomly selected prompts that were not included during pre-training across various GPT variants. Our findings reveal that performance on these unseen prompts is significantly lower than on standard benchmark tests, supporting the conclusion that LLMs are confined to their trained domains rather than mastering a general domain.

Let $p$ be an odd prime. This work develops an application of Hida theory to $p$-adic representations of the $p$-adic integers that are $p$-irrregular up to a fixed scalar. It establishes the identification of $p$-rregular submodules for such representations by linking them to the Hida family and demonstrating a $p$-adic continuity across the geometry of the eigencurve.

While the deep learning framework for Rydberg atom-based measurements has been established, its resilience to environmental noise remains unclear. This study introduces a deep learning approach for distinguishing Rydberg atom states in a noisy environment, where the signal represents a superposition of a Rydberg atom superposition and noise. We demonstrate that deep learning outperforms traditional maximum-likelihood estimation, particularly in high noise scenarios, effectively suppressing noise interference. Furthermore, we validate the model experimentally using a noisy superposition state of two Rydberg atoms, where results match theoretical predictions. Finally, we conclude that deep learning offers a robust, effective method for characterizing the quantum states of Rydberg atom ensembles under noisy conditions.

**Context:** The study of H\_{\rm II} regions in nearby spiral galaxies is essential for understanding their characteristics and their role in the broader context of star formation.

**Aims:** We aim to investigate the properties of H\_{\rm II} region populations in UGC 8839, a nearby (13.5 Mpc) Scd-type spiral galaxy.

**Methods:** We utilized archival data from the Spitzer Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) and the Spitzer Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) to derive the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of H\_{\rm II} region candidates. These SEDs were then employed to determine the electron number density ($N_e$), ionizing star count ($N_{\star}$), and the number of ionizing stars per unit luminosity ($N_{\star}/L$).

**Results:** Our analysis indicates that the median H\_{\rm II} region in UGC 8839 has an electron number density of $N_e = 100$ cm$^{-3}$ and an ionizing star count of $N_{\star} = 10^{40}$ s$^{-1}$. Additionally, the distribution of these objects follows a power-law relationship with a slope of $\alpha = -1.5$ in galactocentric radii. This radial trend is notably steeper than those observed in other spiral

We analyze the dynamics of a family of quasiregular maps self-applied to the 3-sphere, $ Q_{\varepsilon} $, which are conjugate via an isometry to the Böttcher map of a family of real analytic quasiregular maps on $ \mathbb{R}^3 $, denoted $ f_{\varepsilon} $. For each $ f_{\varepsilon} $, there exists a unique compact invariant set, $ J_{\varepsilon} $, which is the image under the Böttcher conjugacy of the closed unit ball in $ \mathbb{R}^3 $; this set $ J_{\varepsilon} $ constitutes the quasiregular Julia set. By analyzing the behavior of the dimension of $ J_{\varepsilon} $ as a function of the parameter $ \varepsilon $, we establish the differentiability of the map $ \varepsilon \mapsto \text{dim}_H(J_{\varepsilon}) $ and provide upper bound estimates for its derivative.

The study utilizes data from the Mars Atmosphere and Global Evolution Experiment (MAGEE) on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter to analyze the relationship between gravity wave (GW) activity and temperature in the Martian upper atmosphere (15–100 km). MAGEE's limb-sounding capability provides vertical profiles of temperature and aerosols, which are employed to derive horizontal GW wavelengths from the 2006–2010 period. These results indicate that, on average, GW vertical wavelengths shorten with increasing altitude; however, this trend is not uniform across all atmospheric layers. Specifically, below 40 km, GW vertical wavelengths correlate positively with horizontal wavelengths, whereas above 40 km, this correlation disappears. Furthermore, the research examines the timing of GW dissipation in the lower atmosphere, finding a strong link between temperature variability and limb-derived aerosol variability between 20 and 30 km, which points to the significant role of gravity waves in driving atmospheric dynamics in this region.

Heavy vector mesons are predominantly produced in photoprocesses at the LHC, with quarkonia and $J/\psi$ serving as the heaviest examples. In the context of vector-mesdom dominance, the production of these states proceeds via the exchange of a vector meson's reggeized photon equivalent. This paper investigates the impact of heavy vector mesons on vector-mesdom dominance within vector-mesdom processes at the LHC, specifically examining the $\pi^0$ production channel alongside the $\rho$, $\Upsilon$, and $\psi$ sectors. Our analysis indicates that heavy vector mesons exert a significant influence on $\pi^0$ production in the forward region at the LHC, whereas their contribution to the $\rho$, $\psi$, and $\Upsilon$ channels is negligible.

Fully connected Recurrent Neural Networks (FCRNNs) are notoriously difficult to train, often resulting in vanishing or exploding gradients. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks were developed to address this issue by mitigating gradient explosion or vanishing through careful gate management. However, this solution introduces significant challenges related to vanishing information, which hampers the network's ability to retain long-term dependencies. This study presents a new network design that outperforms FCRNNs and standard recurrent variants in both accuracy and training speed. The model is grounded in a new design principle for constructing effective dependency graphs, utilizing a graph-based learning rule to identify the optimal structure. This approach also employs an innovative learning strategy to acquire node and edge weights. The resulting architecture, the Dependency Graph-based Recurrent Neural Network (DGRNN), mimics the selective information flow of established models like FCRNNs, LSTMs, and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) but operates more efficiently. Empirical results demonstrate that DGRNN achieves superior performance and faster training times across various tasks, including character, digit, and sentiment analysis, as well as stock market prediction.

This study develops a differential game framework to investigate the optimal strategies for controlling the spread of COVID-19. Our model incorporates two policy instruments: a "moderate" measure that balances medical efficacy against economic impact, and a "strict" measure applied exclusively for medical benefits. These strategies are selected based on the current state of infection. We prove that the differential game possesses a unique solution for optimal strategies, which are derived through forward-backward stochastic differentiation. Our findings indicate that implementing policies in accordance with infection levels is indeed optimal. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the specific choice between a strict and a moderate response is most critical when infection levels are low or high. The proposed theory is applicable to real-world scenarios, such as the pandemic in the Indian state of Maharashtra.

This paper presents DataScope, an interactive environment designed for streamlined debugging of machine learning (ML) data. Scope into the root causes of ML model deficiencies often requires visual inspection and manipulation of datasets, yet current tools struggle to support this with large-scale, complex data (e.g., images, audio, video) effectively. Existing solutions typically rely on notebook-based custom code or generic visualization platforms, both of which hinder users from efficiently navigating and exploring vast, multi-modal structures.

To address these challenges, DataScope offers a specialized data browser equipped with programmatic controls tailored for data debugging tasks. It enables users to rapidly navigate and explore datasets through the lens of machine learning pipelines, specifically allowing for the identification and correction of data issues that stem from downstream processing steps. By facilitating quick navigation and manipulation, DataScope significantly accelerates the discovery and fixing of such problems. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach accelerates data debugging activities by a factor of 3.5x compared to traditional alternatives.

Mn$_3$Sn is a leading candidate for high-mobility antiferromagnetic semimetals, yet its intrinsic low-energy properties remain poorly understood. This study employs density functional theory (DFT) to explore these aspects, revealing that the low-energy electronic structure closely mirrors that of the higher-symmetry hexagonal structure, which has been experimentally confirmed. We further analyze the mechanisms behind the observed anomalous Hall effect in this semimetal. Our findings suggest the effect stems from a combination of trimerization and an anisotropic Fermi surface, a perspective that offers new insights into recent experimental data. Additionally, we examine how magnetic impurities influence the low-energy band structure, a crucial factor for understanding spintronic devices. This work provides a robust theoretical basis for advancing research on Mn$_3$Sn.

Recent years have witnessed a significant surge in Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based approaches to Relation Extraction (RE), a critical task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that aims to identify relational associations between entities within text. While these methods have proven highly effective, they remain vulnerable to overfitting, a challenge that necessitates strategies such as regularization. This paper introduces a novel regularization technique for enhancing DNN-driven RE systems: the Dynamic Batch Normalization (DBN) layer. By adapting the principles of Batch Normalization and incorporating it as a final layer within the network, our method dynamically scales and shifts layer outputs to maintain a consistent distribution, thereby suppressing overfitting. Experiments conducted on two RE datasets reveal that this approach surpasses existing regularized DNN models and yields favorable comparisons against leading architectures for RE and NLP tasks.

In this work, we examine the Steklov-Robin problem where the domain is constructed by removing a ball of radius $r$ from an otherwise unbounded region containing that ball. We evaluate the limits of the first eigenvalue, the corresponding first eigenfunction, and the spectral gap as the removed ball's radius approaches both zero and infinity. We also look at the sensitivities of the first eigenvalue regarding the radius $r$ and the Robin parameter, analyzing how variations in these variables impact the value.

Graph data analysis frequently involves scenarios where direct access to the original graph is impossible, relying instead on multiple projections of it. A central challenge in this context is reconstructing the underlying graph or its projections through these observations. When dealing with hypergraphs, however, direct reconstruction often fails due to the sparsity of non-zero entries in their adjacency matrices. Consequently, existing approaches typically rely on edge-weighted adjacency matrices, where an edge connects any pair of vertices and its value reflects the count of original hyperedges linking those vertices. This study addresses the problem of recovering a simple, unweighted hypergraph from its projection in a setting with no prior knowledge of the graph's structural parameters, specifically its rank (length) or rank distribution. We propose a statistical model to represent such data and establish upper bounds regarding the complexity of possible rank structures. Furthermore, we introduce an algorithm designed to the recover the hypergraph from its weighted projection. Our method assumes a uniform distribution of vertex labels and assumes that edge weights in the projection follow a multinomial distribution. Theoretically, we demonstrate the statistical consistency of our recovery approach and provide explicit sample complexity requirements. Experimentally, we evaluate the algorithm's efficacy on both synthetic datasets and real-world data.

This paper introduces the PAXRay dataset, which enhances visual grounding in radiology by linking 3000+ 3D CT scans to 1,000+ visualized ground truth annotations. These descriptions, sourced from expert radiological reports, detail anatomical structures and pathologies with precise spatial accuracy. To achieve this, we developed an automated pipeline that generates high-quality 2D image slices and their corresponding ground truth projections from the 3D data. This resource facilitates advanced research into medical image understanding, specifically targeting semantic reasoning and visual grounding within medical imaging.

This paper provides counterexamples to a conjecture by Sotak, which suggested that every integral second cohomology class with a unit norm can manifest as the Euler class of an sm-foliation on certain manifolds. Our sm-examples demonstrate this by showing the validity of the above hypothesis only on specific manifolds.
