Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become highly influential in machine learning, particularly for solving node classification tasks on various graph structures. Although standard CNNs and fully connected (FC) neural networks can be reformulated as specific instances of GCNs, GCNs typically rely on sparse, task-specific adjacency matrices that reflect domain knowledge. This reliance creates limitations regarding the generalization to data with different structures. To address this, we introduce a new class of GCNs utilizing a self-optimizing, generalizable adjacency matrix. Our approach employs the Generalized Random Walk framework to derive these adjacency relationships, effectively linking GCNs to the principles of Invariance and Equivariance in machine learning. Empirical results demonstrate that this methodology outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches across multiple benchmark datasets.

Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST) is an algorithm designed to create self-training protocols for parsing tasks, leveraging parsed structures as semi-supervised training data to enhance model performance. While effective, traditional self-training often struggles with two key limitations: an inability to capture long-range dependencies and a tendency to overconfidently train on noisy data. To address these shortcomings, we present a refined self-training approach that integrates parsed structures with semi-supervised techniques, specifically noise selection and distillation. This new framework, also called DCST, functions as follows: first, it generates initial structure predictions using a teacher model; second, it iteratively refines these predictions by replacing ground truth parsing labels with the generated structures. This iterative process is achieved through three core steps: (1) expanding ground truth structures to create an initial training pool, (2) selecting the most probable candidate structures from this expanded set to form a final training pool, and (3) applying a student-teacher mechanism where student models learn from both ground truth data and the teacher's structure predictions. Experiments conducted on two standard dependency parsing datasets demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

A collection of n numbers under comparison forms an n-tuple, classified as nontransitive if at least one of its pairwise subsets constitutes a cyclic relationship. This paper presents the explicit construction of a n-tuple where every possible nonempty subset experiences exactly one cyclic permutation. Specifically, this construction is valid whenever n is a composite number, while excluding the cases where n equals 3 or any prime number.

The proliferation of options in systems like compilers and interpreters has significantly boosted their popularity, yet this trend also complicates the identification and elimination of unused run-time options. Such idle settings can cause security vulnerabilities, degrade performance, and erode system stability. This study introduces "OptionMiner," a novel tool designed to pinpoint dormant run-time options across various systems. By analyzing source code, the option identification process is simplified, making it more efficient than previously available methods. The tool was evaluated on three prominent compilers, revealing a total of 1,015 unused run-time options. The authors have made these discovered unused options publicly available at https://optionminer.github.io.

This study investigates how dark matter-nucleus scattering within a detector volume can be identified through ionization, even when the resulting recoil is too minimal to cause direct track displacement at the microscopic scale. The detection mechanism relies on observing lateral spreading of the track, or blurring, which stems from multiple low-momentum recoils by dark matter particles. We propose using image analysis techniques to quantify this blurring and estimate the transverse momentum transferred to the nucleus. We demonstrate that, for certain assumptions regarding dark matter properties, this approach through image analysis can enhance the sensitivity of an existing experimental setup by several orders of magnitude compared to traditional detection methods, effectively allowing the observation of ionization from low-momentum transfers that would otherwise go unnoticed.

Quantum teleportation enables the transmission of an arbitrary unknown quantum state from one distant location to another via quantum entanglement. In this study, we analyze a standard teleportation setup utilizing a quantum well coupled to a single-mode cavity, operating within the quantum electrodynamics of moving bodies (QMQMB) framework and accounting for realistic effects such as spontaneous emission and atomic decay. We evaluate end-to-end fidelity for teleported anti-polariton qubits entangled in anti-symmetric (A) and anti-helical (R) polarization configurations. Compared to an ideal scenario ignoring spontaneous emission, high fidelity is achieved near the cavity resonance when the detuning is minimal, provided spontaneous emission and photon spontaneous emission rates are balanced. Specifically, at a detuning matching the sum of these decay rates, fidelity is expected to be high. Our numerical analysis reveals that considering spontaneous emission generally yields superior fidelity compared to models that neglect it, particularly for both A and R polarization modes under large detuning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that quantum teleportation of the anti-helical mode achieves higher fidelity than the anti-symmetric mode across various polarization and detuning conditions. These findings suggest that quantum well–single-mode cavity systems serve as a promising platform for efficient teleportation of anti-polariton qubits while accounting for spontaneous emission.

Extracting inter-beat intervals (IBIs) from noisy electrocardiogram (ECG) data is a critical initial phase in heart rate variability (HRV) analysis. Conventional signal processing techniques rely on identifying ECG peaks, yet these often produce erroneous IBI estimates when the input data contains noise. This study introduces a deep-learning technique to model the non-linear relationship between ECG waveforms and IBIs. ECG signals were sourced from the Physionet MIT-BIH training datasets, and deep neural networks were trained to predict precise IBIs. The resulting network demonstrated high accuracy, yielding a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0056 seconds and a coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of 0.9990. Furthermore, the approach was tested on a small set of ECGs from healthy participants to validate its real-world applicability. The findings indicate that this proposed method offers a robust, accurate, and adaptable solution for generating ECG-derived IBIs, particularly beneficial for noisy clinical environments.

This study investigates the statistical fluctuations of active forces driving a particle through a space-dependent potential, employing both Monte Carlo simulations and anharmonic stochastic simulation algorithms. By calculating the autocorrelation functions for various active force models, we demonstrate that fluctuations follow a power-law decay for both harmonic and anharmonic potentials, indicating long-term memory. However, anharmonic force characteristics significantly alter this memory profile. Furthermore, we present a closed-form analytical formula for the mean squared displacement (MSD) applicable to general one-dimensional active force scenarios and extend this analysis to three-dimensional periodic systems.

> "This study introduces Multilingual Continual Learning (MCL), a new task involving the incremental training of a multilingual model where new languages are added over time. We address two primary hurdles: (1) adding languages sequentially without access to a large corpus of labeled data for every single one, and (2) enhancing the performance of all supported languages continuously. To overcome these issues, we propose a data-free, self-structured self-supervised learning approach. This method trains a self-supervised pre-linguaged model for each newly introduced language, which is then seamlessly integrated into the existing multilingual mixture by developing a specialized freezing fine-tuning strategy. Experiments conducted on the CoRAL benchmark demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving many added languages. An effective approach to video super-resolution (Video SR) must handle two key factors: the non-causal nature of errors and motion estimation. While previous works like basic video SR (BasicVSR) addressed these issues through unrolled temporal consistency, they relied on iterative optimization that resulted in high computational costs and limited performance gains. To overcome this, we introduce BasicVSR+, a method that maintains the non-causal temporal consistency of the original framework but eliminates iteration through direct regression. This iterative-free approach improves both speed and performance, yielding higher PSNR scores and faster processing times than BasicVSR. Additionally, we implement cross-scale consistency to enhance high-frequency details, yielding further PSNR gains without additional complexity. The resulting model, named BasicVSR+ with Cross-scale Consistency (CV), outperforms current non-iterative temporal consistent methods on the VIDEOSR2019 dataset.

Dynamic models are pivotal for predicting future states, a capability often leveraged to facilitate reinforcement learning (RL) across multiple tasks. However, existing approaches typically struggle to simultaneously support effective prediction and control, or they restrict prediction capabilities to specific control policies. In this study, we present a novel RL task-agnostic dynamics model trained to generate future state predictions. We observe that employing a monolithic model for all tasks in a multi-task RL setting can detrimentally impact performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a model ensemble technique inspired by model-based methods, enabling an RL agent to select from multiple dynamic predictors. Our approach leverages an encoder to learn a shared dynamics model per task and a dedicated controller to execute the optimal action selection based on task requirements. Empirical evaluations across a RL framework involving multiple tasks demonstrate a significant boost in returns by utilizing an ensemble of dynamic models tailored to each specific task.

We examine a general, spatially discrete heat engine with $N$ sites, interacting with two heat baths at distinct temperatures, $\beta^{-1}_L$ and $\beta^{-1}_R$, while being driven out of equilibrium by a current of $J$ and a scaling parameter $\lambda$. We demonstrate that the engine's performance is governed by $\lambda/N$, implying that reducing system size enhances performance. Furthermore, by analyzing two specific models, we find that optimizing the scaling parameter maximizes the output-to-input power ratio when $\lambda \sim 1$. This implies that heat engines based on fewer components exhibit superior scaling.

This study examines the effects of past and historical hurricanes on the power grid, utilizing the grid's physical structure alongside historical storm paths. By integrating actual hurricane tracks with historical data, the research evaluates grid impacts and develops a method to assess the probability of future hurricane occurrences.

This paper demonstrates the generalization of Hadamard's Three Circles Theorem to a proof involving positive linear functionals, as defined within a space of continuous functions over the compact metric space $[0,1]^n$. From this generalized theorem, we derive a corresponding generalization of Hadamard's Lemma regarding three squares for monogenic functions in higher-dimensional settings.

We introduce two families of lower shift-free, marked maps that serve as generalizations of the Markovian cutting map. Their associated coding spaces exhibit a direct relationship with the Dyck language system and can be mapped via homomorphisms to specific sub-Dyck languages. Furthermore, we establish algorithms for determining both lexicographically minimal and canonical codings within these frameworks.

Model parameters for scenarios featuring extended scalar sectors can be rigorously constrained using data from high-luminosity colliders. This study examines the sensitivity of high-luminosity Interferometer for Muon Colliders (IMC) and the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) in diagnosing electroweak phase transitions within the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM). The analysis evaluates the discriminatory power of various observables, including scalar mass spectra, Higgs couplings to fermions and gauge bosons, as well as the strength and dynamics of the EEWPT. The findings indicate that an IML outperforms the HL-LHC in probing 2HDM parameters and phase transition characteristics, primarily due to the cleaner environment and higher energy capabilities of the proposed muon collider.

This paper introduces Quasi-Periodic Deep Networks (QP-DNs), a newly proposed architecture designed to model quasi-periodic signals, with a primary focus on speech. The T-Net, a fundamental building block of the QP-DN, utilizes three parameters—representing the offset, frequency, and amplitude of a quasi-periodic function—to model the speech pitch cycle. These parameters are refined through back-propagation alongside standard neural network forward propagation. We validate the T-Net's capability to accurately model speech pitch cycles using the speech database. Furthermore, the paper presents two cascaded QP-DN models, V-QP-DN and D-QP-DN, which employ multiple T-Blocks in series to independently model speech pitch cycles at different frequencies. The results demonstrate that these cascaded structures effectively model speech at a multi-pitch resolution, achieving accuracy comparable to the traditional auto-correlation method.

Collaborative Filtering (CF) is a well-established technique for predicting missing ratings in recommendation systems. Recently, biclustering-based CF approaches have emerged, aiming to group similar users and items by identifying relevant submatrices (biclusters) within the rating matrix to generate recommendations. While these methods improve accuracy, they often struggle with prediction confidence, as the magnitude of relevant values within a bicluster alone may not reliably indicate prediction certainty. To address this limitation, we introduce a new unsupervised bicluster-based CF framework termed USBFC. This approach enhances confidence by integrating user and item similarity directly into the relevance of a submatrix. Specifically, USBFC operates in two stages: first, it constructs biclusters by simultaneously optimizing the relevance of values and the similarity of users and items within those groups; second, it utilizes these biclusters for predictions. By simulating user and item similarities during the initial phase, USBFC ensures a more holistic determination of relevance. Our findings demonstrate that USBFC outperforms existing biclustering CF techniques in terms of prediction confidence and overall performance.

Magnetic activity on exoplanet-host stars influences the atmospheric evolution of their planetary systems. While activity indicators such as the H$\alpha$ line and the F10.2nm flux index are commonly used to characterize stellar magnetic behavior, they may lack the sensitivity to capture specific phenomena like spots or flares. This study proposes that the equivalent width (EW) of the Ca II infrared triplet lines—measured via the index log $R_{HK}$—provides a more effective tracer of surface magnetic activity. By analyzing the Gaia-ESO Survey data for 1,000 M-dwarf stars, we demonstrate that Ca II triplet-based log $R_{HK}$ correlates with the H$\alpha$ line index log $R_H$ and the activity index $\Delta$10.2nm derived from the $\lambda$10230Å band. Our findings indicate that the Ca II triplet is a more efficient indicator of general magnetic activity than the H$\alpha$ line. Additionally, we examine the relationship between these indices and the planet's orbital period, revealing that the indices log $R_{HK}$ and log $R_H$ are independent of the period, whereas the $\Delta$10.2nm index shows a clear correlation with it. Finally, we compare the derived $\Delta$10.2nm index with the $\Delta$H$\alpha$ index, observing that the former is more sensitive to variations in stellar mass and age.

This study examines zero-energy spectral features in microwave reflection experiments involving Majorana modes within Miessner wires. We demonstrate that a pronounced peak observed at zero energy—which arises from non-Majorana mechanisms—is significantly suppressed when the system operates at finite temperatures or传输 energies. Conversely, genuine signatures of Majorana modes can persist under these same non-ideal conditions. This clear distinction enables zero-energy resonance peaks to serve as a diagnostic tool for differentiating Majorana states from alternative explanations.

We establish a general method for constructing a "shadow" within the bicategorical setting of an $A_\infty$-2-category, which we then apply to derive the topological Hochschild homology of a ring spectrum as well as its associated 2-category. This framework furthermore yields the "2-typed" structure of torus Hochschild homology and the "2-typed" structure of the associated algebra.

We introduce a novel method for extracting style from images, denoted as iStyle, which outperforms established techniques such as PCA or VAE in the resulting style space. Unlike these traditional approaches, iStyle encodes image style through the specific arrangement of spatial frequency components, a process that functions as a spatially aware principal component analysis. By performing PCA on the spatial domain rather than the global image representation, the method captures how style patterns vary across an image, leading to more accurate and nuanced stylistic encoding.

This study introduces a new approach to video feature representation, grounded in a hybrid architecture combining a module convolutional neural network with ground module attention. The proposed framework, named Video Module Attention Network (V-MAN), utilizes the Spatio-Temporal Module (STM) to capture local features across spatial and temporal dimensions. These features are subsequently refined through the application of ground module attention, which incorporates context ground information to focus on the most relevant modules for a given frame. The resulting ground module attention maps effectively highlight the most pertinent features within the video sequence. The proposed method is validated on two datasets, MSR-Vide and Movie Description, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance. The source code can be accessed at the following URL: https://github.com/ysj1996/V-MAN.

This study investigates the settling of finite-sized, neutrally buoyant, soft, and deformable particles within turbulent flows, with a specific focus on applications to snowpack erosion. By employing a large-scale numerical simulation framework, we model these particles using a novel, computationally efficient framework based on a quasi-static approach that integrates a continuum description of snow rheology. Validation against experimental data for settling velocities in quiescent conditions demonstrates good agreement, particularly in the intermediate inertia regime. When examining turbulence, we observe that for Stokes numbers ranging from 0.01 to 1, turbulent fluctuations enhance settling velocity by up to 40% compared to still fluid conditions. Furthermore, to ensure the robustness of these findings, we compared our results with two alternative models: one treating particles as rigid spheres and another assuming rigid particles subject to overpressure deformation. These comparisons confirm the reliability of our proposed framework.

Although recent deep learning breakthroughs have significantly advanced our ability to model the complex, high-dimensional distributions of sensory data like images, audio, and video, these technologies are constrained by their reliance on massive quantities of real, labeled data. This paper presents a solution to this limitation through a new framework for training world models using exclusively synthetic data. By integrating a data generation pipeline with a novel architecture for world modeling, our system creates realistic sequences of states and transitions that mirror the characteristics of complex, high-dimensional environments. This synthetic training data is then leveraged to build model-based agents capable of navigating such worlds effectively. We validate the approach across two distinct tasks: first, in a navigation scenario where an agent operates within a figure-skating world, and second, in a robotic manipulation setting where a robot handles an egg. These experiments demonstrate that agents trained on simulated data achieve performance on par with those trained on real data when evaluated in actual robotic manipulation tasks.

For a given pair of geometric hypergraphs $\mathcal{H}$ and $\mathcal{F}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is not present in $\mathcal{H}$, the saturation problems focus on determining the saturation numbers. These numbers represent the maximum number of edges in a geometric hypergraph that avoids $\mathcal{F}$ within $\mathcal{H}$ but remains minimally saturated, meaning the removal of any single edge would allow $\mathcal{F}$ to appear. While research into these problems for basic cases has been active for some time, progress has historically been limited. This paper presents the inaugural solution for specific nontrivial instances. The authors provide the exact saturation numbers when $\mathcal{F}$ is a convex matching of three edges and $\mathcal{H}$ is either the complete geometric convex $4$-graph or the convex Monge graph, considering both convex matchings and general configurations of points in the plane.

The study investigates the formation of bound nuclei via direct reactions on light targets, specifically analyzing the $^{16}$O + $^4$He collisions with $^{14}$N, $^{13}$C, and $^{12}$C targets at a laboratory energy of 240 Me/nucleon. This energy level is high enough to allow the application of the Impulse Approximation, enabling the impulse-approximation production cross-sections for alpha particles to be derived from experimental removal cross-sections data for single nucleons from the resulting bound states. A comparable analysis was performed for deuteron formation using existing, comparable $^{16}$O + $d$ data at the same 240 MeV. The results indicate that, at this energy, producing an alpha particle via this channel is roughly a thousand times more probable than producing a deuteron. Furthermore, the findings suggest a correlation between the binding energy of the formed nucleus and its production cross-section.

This paper introduces *Trident*, a Pacific Lamprey-inspired climbing robot designed to navigate rough vertical surfaces. *Trident* features a 30 cm length and utilizes three actuated, anisotropic, helical propulsion segments. By applying tractive forces through self-propelled rotation, these segments enable the robot to climb. This study examines the influence of individual segment rotation speeds and inter-segment spacing on the robot's performance. Optimal configurations were identified, achieving a peak climbing velocity of 20 cm/s. For comparison, the average swimming speed of a 30 cm Pacific lamprey is approximately 2.5 cm/s, indicating that *Trident*'s ascent is eight times faster than the animal's forward motion in water.

Doxorubicin (Dox) is a prodrug that, once internalized by cells, is converted into its active form, Doxol (Doxol). This study examines how Doxol influences the tumor microenvironment by triggering the release of Interleukin-2 (IL-2), a key cytokine. We present a mathematical model of host-tumor interactions incorporating these mechanisms and perform sensitivity analyses on parameter variations. Our simulation results indicate that combination therapy using both IL-2 and Doxorubicin is more effective than either treatment alone, successfully driving the tumor toward extinction while stabilizing T-cell levels within physiological ranges.

This study investigates the relationship between the freshness of information, measured as Age of Information (AoI), and wireless throughput. Specifically, it examines how throughput-maximizing policies influence average AoI, noting a generally adverse trade-off where higher throughput tends to degrade information freshness. Conversely, we demonstrate an AoI-throughput synergy within point-to-point block fading channels. Under certain conditions, it is possible for the throughput-maximizing transmission policy to simultaneously achieve the lowest possible average AoI. These findings are established by explicitly and tightly bounding both metrics as functions of transmission power, alongside the derivation of critical power thresholds. Consequently, the research shows that, rather than following the typical compromise, the very same strategy can optimally address both AoI and throughput in specific scenarios.

Relatedness takes on different meanings across the fields of geometrical optics and spectral theory. This paper examines two such parallels: one connecting the decay of potentials with compact connection, and another linking the behavior of eigenvalues to that of snare drum eigenfunctions. We achieve a more precise understanding of these relationships by deriving sharper asymptotic formulas. Specifically, we prove a more accurate version of the Dyson-Lieb-Thirring inequality for potentials that are compactly supported, yielding a tighter link between a potential's compactness and its eigenvalues. Additionally, we establish an asymptotically exact relationship characteristic of a "more accurate" version of the Weyl law, relating snare drum eigenvalues directly to its vibrating membrane's shape.

We examine the evolution of eccentricity in compact binary systems with moderate eccentricity ($0.1 \lesssim e_0 \lesssim 0.4$) at frequencies detectable by current gravitational-wave interferometers. Our findings indicate that binaries can reach final eccentricities of $e_f \sim 0.1$ at detection thresholds around $10$ Hz, whereas those approaching $25$ Hz retain only $e_f \sim 0.01$. These results demonstrate that binaries detectable by both Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo may exhibit measurable eccentricity, whereas those detectable by third-generation detectors like Einstein Telescope and Cosmological Explorer likely will not. We also establish that the amplitudes of the harmonic components in the gravitational-wave spectrum for moderately eccentric binaries are comparable to or exceed those from circular binaries of the same chirp mass and luminosity distance. Consequently, current data analysis pipelines, which rely on the circular binary approximation, could miss detectable sources or yield biased parameter estimates. To address this, we urge the immediate development of efficient templates encompassing eccentricity corrections.

Graph generation models have garnered significant attention for their ability to capture graph distribution and facilitate downstream tasks like link prediction and link. However, event detection remains a distinct and vital challenge, yet existing approaches are limited by their reliance on static graph snapshots, which hinder the detection of events in dynamic environments. To address this, we introduce DyGED, the first end-to-end model designed to generate and analyze event dynamics directly within dynamic graphs. Unlike traditional methods that process static structures, DyGED operates on time-evolving graphs to identify correlations between temporal graph patterns and event sequences. It achieves this through two core mechanisms: (1) a time-aware encoder that extracts dependencies within dynamic graphs, and (2) a dedicated link generator that infers relationships between these patterns and specific events. For validation, we conducted comprehensive experiments on two real-world dynamic datasets, comparing the model's performance against state-of-the-art techniques. The results demonstrate that DyGED significantly outperforms existing methods in accuracy. Furthermore, ablation studies were performed to evaluate the individual contributions of the link generator and the link filter (or the impact of different filtering strategies on event processing).

The paper introduces a novel method for numerically solving Guderley self-similar problem cases, covering both ablation-driven scenarios with power-law profiles and laser ablation mechanisms involving inverse-square laws in the context of spherical symmetry. These exact solutions are designed to help hydrodynamic coders validate their simulations, especially when simulating the early stages of spherical implosion where ablation pressure acts on the inwardly accelerating shell. We specifically address the need for improved accuracy in simulations by enhancing the treatment of ablation boundary conditions, a factor that existing models often handle inadequately. We propose applying flux filtering to smooth the spatial distribution of ablation pressure and mass loss rates near the boundary, a technique shown to significantly enhance simulation fidelity. We extend this filtering approach to encompass general, arbitrary ablation profiles.

The rise of Deep Learning has enabled AI systems to achieve remarkable performance across numerous domains, yet these models function as "black boxes" that struggle to provide understandable reasoning for their outputs. This limitation poses significant challenges for applications requiring accountability, such as those within the legal system or medical fields. The objective of this paper is to explore how Requirements Engineering (RE) practices and methodologies can drive both the development and adoption of Explainable AI (XAI). We begin by reviewing the current state of RE and XAI before outlining their convergence points. Subsequently, various RE practices were examined to identify opportunities for enhancing XAI through: (1) defining explainability-centric requirements, (2) constructing transparent system models, (3) specifying system behavior via scenario analysis, (4) validating system adherence through testing, and (5) reviewing operational system performance via maintenance activities. Ultimately, various RE practices were explored as avenues for initiating RE-XAI collaboration, and specific strategies for fostering this partnership are presented.

Colorectal cancer ranks as the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States. While regular colonoscopy screenings are vital for early detection, the identification of adenomas is critical because these non-cancerous growths can progress into colorectal cancer. This study introduces a deep neural network approach to not only classify adenomas but also perform a one-step, automated H&G grading process. Adenoma detection during colonoscopy relies on visual assessment of a polyp's surface characteristics, such as its texture and color, which are analyzed in this work. Using a dataset of 1,000 high-resolution, full-color colonoscopic images annotated by pathologists, the adenomas were first categorized into three groups: tubular, serrated, or other. Following this classification, an adenoma classifier and a grade predictor were developed to assign images to specific histological grades based on whether they are low-grade or high-grade. The results indicate a classification accuracy of 88.2% and a grade prediction R² score of 0.753. These metrics demonstrate that, with continued refinement, these deep learning models have the potential to assist clinicians in precise, automated decision-making for adenoma management.

We introduce a hierarchical deep-generative model, called Multi-scale SAR image Arrangement by Relational Priors (MrSARP), designed to syneticate high-, medium-, and low-resolution synthetic SAR images. This end-to-end approach generates data hierarchically, moving from coarsest to finest resolutions, effectively solving the inefficiencies of traditional single-resolution generation methods that struggle to produce multi-scale datasets. Our architecture integrates a variational auto-encoder with a relational network to first recover latent data representations and then reconstruct the corresponding images. Evaluations demonstrate that MrSARP achieves superior image quality and lower generation costs compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) represents a prominent framework for tackling variational optimization challenges using quantum computing. However, QAOA faces criticism regarding its reliance on inefficient, iterative parameter tuning. In this study, we introduce a method to enhance QAOA performance by leveraging Bayesian optimization to efficiently navigate the variational landscape. The approach begins with a new sampling strategy for constructing an interpolation surrogate model, specifically designed to handle scenarios where evaluation function costs are high. Furthermore, we propose two acquisition functions tailored for scenarios where gradient information regarding the objective function is unavailable. Testing the proposed framework on the Knapsack problem demonstrates that our Bayesian optimization-enhanced QAOA surpasses both standard global search methods and qAOA implementations guided by other heuristics.

Reinforcement learning offers a promising approach for solving the inverse problem of inferring the objective function from which an agent's data is derived. This study examines three distinct actor-critic algorithms to address this challenge: the Fitted Q-Max, Q-Learning, and MaxEnt Reinforcement Learning methods. We demonstrate that each algorithm computes the density function of the Gibbs measure associated with its respective q-function in different ways. Specifically, Fitted Q-Max estimates this density using a parametric assumption, whereas Q-Learning and MaxEnt RL employ a series expansion in absolute error and a random series, respectively. Furthermore, our findings indicate that an agent exhibiting bounded, time-independent q-functions and following a Gaussian policy will result in a Gibbs measure density that follows a Gaussian distribution, whereas agents using other learning algorithms will generate Gibbs measures with support across the entire state-action space.

Although the physical nature of high-$T_c$ superconductivity remains elusive, it is broadly accepted that the underlying mechanism stems from electron-electron correlations in the Hubbard model. While it is established that long-range order is suppressed by these correlations, we demonstrate that the system can instead settle into stable striped phases, driven by quantum fluctuations. Specifically, we show that in one-dimensional half-filled Hubbard chains, the ground state exhibits a spatial modulation of both charge and spin orders. Furthermore, these modulation patterns in 2D and higher dimensions lead to experimentally testable signatures. Our findings reveal that stripe phases can emerge even with moderate interaction strengths, offering promising avenues for theoretical and experimental investigation into high-$T_c$ superconductors.

Identifying vertebrae from medical images is vital for numerous clinical applications, yet it remains difficult due to the subtle inter-vertebral variations, irregular organ shapes, and imaging artifacts inherent in such data. Current state-of-the-art techniques typically rely on complex, lossy data augmentation strategies or data-centric approaches to tackle this challenge. This paper introduces a novel, unsupervised domain adaptation method designed to enhance vertebra identification by utilizing a CycleGAN to generate realistic, single-view synthesized images from source multi-view scans. These augmented images help mitigate data scarcity and irregular class distributions, while a domain adaptation network is employed to minimize domain discrepancies. Furthermore, to overcome the limitations of lossy preprocessing, a Generative Adaptor is proposed that operates directly on input images using two branches: one for clean feature extraction and another for extracting domain-invariant features by learning feature representations and translating them across domains within the latent space. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in three out of four evaluated datasets, achieving a 3.1% increase in identification accuracy on the ChSpine21 dataset.

This study introduces an algebraic and topological framework for analyzing Markovian models, demonstrating their relevance to the computation of asymptotic averages and correlation integrals using an example-based approach.

This study examines the connection between surface characteristics in piezoelectric materials and their equivalent effective properties. Beginning with the complete transmission constraints across interfaces, we derive the corresponding surface effective piezoelectric and dielectric constants for both single crystals and polycrystalline structures. The analysis reveals that the cross-component of the effective piezoelectric coefficient ($d_{ij}^*$) and the difference between the inverse effective dielectric permittivities ($1/\varepsilon_{ii}^*$) are directly governed by the complete transmission condition. Consequently, we propose a new strategy to design piezoelectric materials with a zero effective $d_{ij}^*$ coefficient by engineering surface properties that nullify the related transmission condition. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface elasticity can be utilized to manipulate effective dielectric behavior, a finding with significant implications for surface engineering and the design of piezoelectric devices.

Polariton condensates within semiconductor microcavities, which represent the lowest-energy eigenstates of the system, exhibit characteristics determined by the matrix elements of the Hamiltonian. Since the matrix elements are governed by the spatial light modulation of the excitation beams, varying the excitation light patterns allows for the control of condensate properties. This research demonstrates that using such techniques, specifically a "dumbbell" shaped excitation beam, enables the twisting of a single connected polariton condensate. The resulting dynamics are explained through a model that incorporates the polariton's complex nature, accounting for both phase and density.

The described phase-wrapping mechanism relies on a particular aspect ratio of the dumbbell shape, creating a relative phase gradient between the two lobes. This creates a complex order parameter with a constant phase gradient along the connection, resulting in a spiral pattern of the condensate's density. We conducted a study on the potential atmospheric evaporation of the planet K2-22 b, a transiting body with an orbital period of 13.7 days around a K4V-type star. Our calculations for mass loss yielded a rate of $1.6 \times 10^{11}$ g/s, which corresponds to a planetary lifetime of approximately 1.1 Gyr. Given the current $5.4 \pm 0.8$ M$_\oplus$ mass estimate for K2-22 b, this implies it will completely evaporate in roughly 4.5 times the age of the universe. We also explored the feasibility of detecting atmospheric signals from this process. Our estimates suggest that the mass loss could generate a neutral hydrogen Ly$\alpha$ excess of $10^{-5}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ Å$^{-1}$ and a water vapor signature of $10^{-13}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ Å$^{-1}$, creating a信噪比 (signal-to-noise ratio) of 3$\sigma$ during a single 10-hour JWST observation.

The collection of homogeneous polynomials with a fixed degree and possibly fixed constants at the origin forms a finite-dimensional vector space. The action of the unitary group, acting as rotations within the ambient Hermitian space, rotates this space. We examine the resulting quotient, which organizes polynomials based on the fiber diffeomorphism type of their Milnor fibration. This classification creates cells that form a poset, with each cell being homeomorphic to a complex convex convex polyhedron. The polyhedron faces correspond to the face lattice of a specific polyhedron, which is itself the Minkowski sum of two fundamental building blocks, which are a simplex and a cyclic polyhedron.

Data analytics frequently relies on the concept of a hash table, a feature available across both Python and C# libraries. Although these environments behave similarly at a high level, implementing hash maps in C# revealed significant differences from Python's dynamic nature. Consequently, we examined the performance and practical usage of four distinct hash map implementations in C# to identify patterns and make informed recommendations for future development.

I argue that Galileo's shift toward scientific method was not driven by his reading of Aristotle's *On the Heavens* and *On Generation and Corruption*, as previously held, but rather by his determination to uphold the rigor of mathematics in science. Although I acknowledge that the works did influence his empirical focus, this specific emphasis on observation had a dual-edged impact: it propelled the development of modern science while simultaneously hindering Galileo's theoretical advancements. I propose that had he balanced his empirical approach with greater theoretical analysis, he might have achieved even greater theoretical success.

A non-Gaussian version of the q-thermodynamic formalism is developed to characterize the statistical properties of a system in contact with a heat bath operating at temperature T, governed by the generalized Gibbs ensemble under the assumption that the system's energy follows a q-Gaussian distribution. The study examines the entropic and geometric characteristics of q-Gaussians within generalized probability spaces defined by a metric parameter (the Hilbert–Schmidt distance), which serves as the inverse q-temperature. By applying the Hahn–Banach theorem and considering q-entropic functionals as q-isometric operators in a Hilbert space, it demonstrates that q-entropic maximization for q-Gaussian distributions is only feasible when q ≤ 1; for values greater than 1, no q-entropic maximization principle exists. Additionally, the concept of q-free energy for q-Gaussians is introduced, revealing a direct link to the q-internal energy and q-binding energy—the latter representing the q-analog of binding energy. The paper concludes by investigating the stability of optimal q-Gaussian distributions and analyzing the spectral properties of q-entropic functionals using q-expectation operators as q-operators within a q-Hilbert space.

This study introduces a new reduced model designed to simulate magnetic island coalescence in tokamaks, a process pivotal to understanding the interaction between large-scale magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and small-scale kinetic physics. The proposed first-order system of partial differential equations incorporates the Frenet–Serret frame alongside an Eulerian coordinate for the radial direction. By integrating reduced kinetic equations for anisotropic velocity distribution functions into this geometric framework, the model effectively captures the physics governing current drive resulting from Coherent Cyclotron Resonance Heating (CCRH) during the island merge phase. The associated mathematical analysis confirms the system's stability solutions exist. Numerical simulations are performed to illustrate the significant impact of reduced kinetic effects on the coalescence dynamics.

Over an extended period, digital helpers must evolve their cognitive strategies and form intuitive responses based on specific human interaction styles. This paper introduces a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework designed to enable a digital helper to cultivate such cognitive strategies and intuitions by partnering with one or multiple humans who each exhibit distinct collaboration methods. We define collaboration methods as varying levels of guidance, ranging from offering no instruction to providing complete step-by-step instructions. This approach allows us to investigate whether an AI agent can effectively adapt its cognitive strategy and generate accurate intuitions about human partners over time, even in scenarios involving the simultaneous discrimination among multiple distinct collaboration styles.
